title: Media Queries
in30Seconds: A CSS media query asks whether a condition about the current environment is true, then lets the browser use a matching set of styles. Most often, the condition concerns available viewport width, but it can also concern output such as print or a user preference such as reduced motion. Put a query on an `@media` rule, and the declarations inside are conditional—not a separate language or a command to detect a particular device.
whyItMatters: Media queries make one stylesheet adapt its presentation to changing conditions without changing the page's HTML or duplicating a site for every screen size. They also support considerate design: a user preference such as reduced motion can select a calmer presentation. In a course, queries clarify how CSS rules become active and how the cascade resolves rules that do match. In practice, writing conditions around content and layout pressure rather than a list of device names produces CSS that is easier to test and maintain.
learningObjectives: Define a CSS media query and the @media rule.
Identify a media type, media feature, and media condition.
Distinguish a minimum-width condition from a maximum-width condition.
Apply a media query that changes a rule only when its condition matches.
Explain why a reduced-motion preference should change non-essential animation rather than remove essential information.

collegeVersion.heading: A conditional group of CSS rules
collegeVersion.body:
A media query is a boolean test about the media environment. CSS can use that test in an `@media` at-rule to make a group of rules conditional. In a stylesheet, the familiar pattern is `@media (width >= 48rem) { ... }`. The declarations inside do not become a new stylesheet and they do not replace the ordinary rules by themselves. Instead, when the condition is true, those declarations participate in the normal cascade alongside any other matching declarations. When it is false, the grouped rules do not apply. That distinction matters when debugging: an apparent failure may be a false condition, an unmatched selector, or a cascade conflict after the condition has matched.

The query can begin with a media type such as `screen` or `print`. It can also test a media feature: `width`, `orientation`, `hover`, `prefers-color-scheme`, and `prefers-reduced-motion` are examples of features with different kinds of values. A query can combine conditions with `and`, negate one with `not`, or use a comma-separated list for alternatives. A list such as `@media print, (width >= 48rem)` matches when either alternative matches. Media queries therefore describe a condition, not a device inventory. A rule based on width means what it says: it tests width; it does not reliably identify a phone, tablet, or laptop.

collegeVersion.heading: Width conditions and readable syntax
collegeVersion.body:
Width is a common feature because available space can create a genuine layout constraint. CSS supports older prefixed forms such as `(min-width: 48rem)` and `(max-width: 47.999rem)`. It also supports range syntax, including `(width >= 48rem)` and a bounded range such as `(30rem <= width < 48rem)`. The two minimum forms express the same threshold idea: the query matches at 48rem or wider. Exact boundary choices are design decisions, not universal breakpoints. A 48rem condition is not a claim that every device at that size has the same needs; it is a rule a particular layout can test.

Consider a navigation component that is ordinarily a vertical list. If a wider inline space makes a horizontal arrangement legible, a matching query can set its list to a row layout. The base CSS should remain meaningful when no width query matches, and the conditional rule should make one explicit, testable change. This lesson does not prescribe a complete responsive strategy or teach a particular layout system. Its point is narrower: a query selects CSS based on a stated condition. Test the threshold by resizing a browser or using responsive tools, then inspect which rule wins. Avoid overlapping conditions that accidentally give competing declarations the same responsibility; when overlap is intentional, understand the cascade order and specificity that decide the result.

collegeVersion.heading: Preferences and non-screen output
collegeVersion.body:
Environment conditions are not only measurements. The `prefers-reduced-motion` media feature reports whether the user has requested reduced non-essential motion. A query such as `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` can shorten or remove decorative transitions and animations. It should not hide information, remove a control's visible state, or make a necessary change impossible to perceive; the goal is to reduce optional motion while preserving meaning and operation. The condition reflects a preference exposed by the user environment, so authors should not treat it as a medical diagnosis or as proof that every visitor needs the same treatment.

Media types make another useful distinction. `@media print` can apply styles while printing or generating print-oriented output: for example, a site may avoid a decorative background or adjust spacing for paper. A print rule is still CSS governed by the same conditional model. It does not automatically make a document print-accessible, and it does not change the HTML's semantic structure. Likewise, media queries are useful alongside semantic HTML, accessible labels, usable focus indicators, and correctly structured content; they do not repair those foundations. Keep the jobs separate. HTML supplies meaning and structure, ordinary CSS supplies base presentation, and media queries select additional or alternative presentation when a documented environment condition matches. This separation makes each decision easier to inspect and revise.

vocabulary.definition: A condition that tests characteristics of the media environment for conditional styling.
A CSS at-rule that conditionally applies its enclosed rules when its media query matches.
A characteristic that a media query can test, such as width, orientation, or a user preference.
A broad output category in a media query, such as screen or print.
A boolean expression made from one or more media-feature tests and logical operators.
Media-query notation that compares a feature with a value, such as width >= 48rem.
A media feature that indicates a user preference to reduce non-essential motion.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Think of ordinary CSS as instructions that are always available: make this text this size, put space here, use this color. A media query adds an “if” label to some instructions. It says, “If the page has at least this much room, use these extra rules,” or “If the person asked for less motion, use the quieter version.” The browser checks the condition and includes those rules only when the answer is yes.

The condition is about the current situation, not the name of a gadget. A narrow browser window on a large computer can meet a narrow-width condition, and a wide window on a small device can meet a wide-width condition. That is why it is more useful to name the condition than to guess the visitor’s hardware.
eli10.analogy: A media query is like a note on a classroom activity box: “Use these materials only if the class is working outdoors.” The activity is still part of the plan, but its condition decides whether it is used.
eli10.analogyLimits: A browser does not make a one-time classroom choice. Conditions can change while a page is open, and matched CSS rules still interact with the cascade, selectors, and other CSS rules.

workedExample: Start with a readable base rule: `.nav { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 0.5rem; }`. Suppose testing shows that the navigation has enough room to become a row at 48rem. Add `@media (width >= 48rem) { .nav { flex-direction: row; } }`. At 47rem, the condition is false, so the column direction remains. At exactly 48rem and above, it is true, so the later matching declaration changes only `flex-direction` to `row`. The query does not create the navigation or identify a device; it selects one presentation rule from an explicit width condition. A separate `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` rule could reduce decorative transition duration without changing the navigation's content or controls.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing a query to identify a specific phone model.
commonMistakes.correction: Test the actual condition the layout needs, such as available width, rather than assuming a device category.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming every @media rule overrides all ordinary CSS.
commonMistakes.correction: A matched rule joins the usual cascade; selector matching, specificity, and order still matter.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a reduced-motion rule to remove essential information or feedback.
commonMistakes.correction: Reduce decorative motion while preserving meaning, controls, and usable state changes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a print query as a substitute for semantic HTML.
commonMistakes.correction: Use print CSS for presentation while keeping the document structurally meaningful in HTML.

compareContrast.distinction: A media query tests the media environment, while a container query can test characteristics of a containing element.
A minimum condition matches at or above its threshold; a maximum condition matches at or below its threshold.
A feature is a specific tested characteristic such as width; a type is a broad category such as print.

keyTakeaway: Media queries are conditional CSS. State the environment condition precisely, keep a usable base style, and remember that a matching @media rule still participates in the normal cascade.

questionBank.prompt: What does an @media rule do when its media query is true?
options: It deletes ordinary CSS rules.
It changes the page's HTML structure.
It lets the rules inside the @media block participate in the CSS cascade.
It permanently stores the viewport width.
questionBank.explanation: A true media query makes the enclosed CSS applicable; HTML and other CSS rules remain, and the cascade still resolves conflicts.
questionBank.skill: Identify the effect of a matching @media rule

questionBank.prompt: Which query matches when the viewport width is at least 48rem?
options: @media (width < 48rem)
@media (width >= 48rem)
@media print
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)
questionBank.explanation: The >= comparison includes 48rem and larger widths. The other options test a narrower width, print media, or a motion preference.

questionBank.prompt: A site has a decorative spinning icon but must preserve the status text beside it. Which conditional rule best respects a visitor who requests reduced motion?
options: Hide the entire status component.
Remove the text and keep the spinner.
Disable all CSS on the page.
Use prefers-reduced-motion to remove or shorten the decorative animation while leaving the status text available.
questionBank.explanation: Reduced-motion styling should reduce non-essential movement while preserving information and operation; hiding content or all CSS does not meet that goal.
questionBank.skill: Apply a user-preference media feature responsibly

questionBank.prompt: Why is @media (width >= 48rem) more accurate than a rule named “tablet mode”?
options: It tests a stated width condition instead of guessing the visitor's device category.
It guarantees a two-column layout is accessible.
It works only on tablets.
It changes the HTML into a tablet-specific document.
questionBank.explanation: The query evaluates width, not device identity. It does not guarantee accessibility, limit itself to tablets, or alter HTML.
questionBank.skill: Separate environment conditions from device labels

questionBank.prompt: What is the effect of the comma in @media print, (width >= 48rem)?
options: Both print and width conditions must be true.
It makes the second condition invalid.
The query matches if either the print type or the width condition matches.
It tests whether a printer is 48rem wide.
questionBank.explanation: A comma-separated media-query list is an OR list. `and`, rather than a comma, combines conditions that must both match.

options: It deletes ordinary CSS rules.
It changes the page's HTML structure.
It lets the rules inside the @media block participate in the CSS cascade.
It permanently stores the viewport width.
quickCheck.explanation: A true media query makes the enclosed CSS applicable; HTML and other CSS rules remain, and the cascade still resolves conflicts.

options: @media (width < 48rem)
@media (width >= 48rem)
@media print
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)
quickCheck.explanation: The >= comparison includes 48rem and larger widths.

options: Hide the entire status component.
Remove the text and keep the spinner.
Disable all CSS on the page.
Use prefers-reduced-motion to remove or shorten the decorative animation while leaving the status text available.

title: JavaScript
in30Seconds: JavaScript is a programming language commonly used in browsers to give a web page behavior. HTML supplies content and structure; CSS describes presentation; JavaScript can respond to changes and user actions, calculate values, or update the interface. It runs in an execution environment, such as a browser tab, and can use browser-provided APIs. JavaScript is not limited to browsers, but this lesson focuses on its client-side web role.
whyItMatters: JavaScript is the layer that makes many web interfaces respond instead of merely display information. Knowing its role helps a developer choose the right tool: revise HTML when meaning or content is wrong, revise CSS when appearance is wrong, and use JavaScript when the page needs behavior. This boundary also makes debugging clearer and prepares you for later work with JavaScript fundamentals, the DOM, events, and network requests.
learningObjectives: Define JavaScript in the context of web development.
Distinguish the roles of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
Explain the browser's role as a client-side JavaScript execution environment.
Identify when a change calls for behavior rather than structure or presentation.
Describe the difference between JavaScript itself and browser APIs it can use.

collegeVersion.heading: A language for behavior
collegeVersion.body:
JavaScript is a programming language. In client-side web development, a browser can execute JavaScript as part of loading and running a page. That makes it useful for behavior: a page can respond when a person chooses a control, update a displayed result after a calculation, or change part of an interface as new information becomes available. Calling JavaScript the “behavior layer” is a useful starting model, but it should not be mistaken for a complete definition of the language. JavaScript can also run outside a browser, including in server environments. This lesson uses the model only to locate JavaScript among the basic web technologies.

The basic division of responsibilities is practical. HTML provides a document's content, structure, and meaning: a button is a button, a heading is a heading, and a paragraph contains text. CSS describes how those document parts are presented: colors, spacing, positioning, and type treatment. JavaScript can decide what should happen at runtime. A button that is visibly styled but does nothing is an HTML-and-CSS result; connecting an appropriate response to an interaction is a JavaScript concern. The layers cooperate, but they are not interchangeable.

This separation supports clear maintenance. If an event notice contains the wrong date, correct the content in HTML or in the system that supplies it. If the notice is difficult to read because of its contrast or spacing, examine CSS. If a “show details” control should reveal already-present details when activated, behavior is the missing piece. A real application can involve more than one layer, so this is not a rule that every change has only one file. It is a way to begin debugging with the right question.

collegeVersion.heading: The browser supplies an execution environment
collegeVersion.body:
A browser tab provides an execution environment for client-side JavaScript. The browser receives page resources, processes HTML and CSS, and can execute scripts associated with the page. JavaScript code does not automatically have every capability a computer has. Instead, the browser offers defined interfaces—browser APIs—that scripts may use according to the platform's rules and the user's permissions. The Document Object Model (DOM) API, for example, represents the page so JavaScript can inspect or change document content, attributes, and styles. The DOM is not the JavaScript language itself; it is a browser-provided API that JavaScript can call.

That distinction prevents a common category error. A language supplies grammar and semantics for expressing computations. A host environment supplies facilities around it. In a browser, those facilities can include page-related APIs, timers, storage, and media interfaces. Another JavaScript environment can expose a different collection. Therefore, “JavaScript can change a page” is shorthand for a more precise statement: JavaScript running in a browser can use browser facilities such as the DOM API to change page-related state. Later lessons will examine the DOM and events directly; for now, keep the language and the host separate.

Browser execution also has boundaries. MDN describes each tab as its own execution environment and explains that code in one tab is generally separated from code in another. This is a helpful security property, not permission for a script to ignore web security rules. A page must still treat data from users and networks carefully, follow browser restrictions, and use appropriate server-side controls. This introductory lesson does not teach security testing or bypasses. Its lesson is architectural: JavaScript runs inside a host with rules, not as unrestricted code floating above the web platform.

collegeVersion.heading: How scripts join a web page
collegeVersion.body:
HTML connects JavaScript to a document with the `script` element. A script can be written in the document or, more commonly for a maintainable project, referenced from a separate JavaScript file. External files make it easier to organize behavior separately from markup and to reuse a script where appropriate. The connection does not erase the role boundaries: HTML still declares that a script belongs to the page, while the script contains behavior.

Loading order matters when code needs a part of the page to exist before the code uses it. Module scripts are deferred by default, meaning their execution waits until the document has been parsed. Other loading approaches have different timing rules. Rather than memorize every attribute here, use the durable principle: understand when the script runs relative to the HTML it needs, and verify behavior in a browser. A later lesson on JavaScript fundamentals and another on the DOM can make that principle concrete.

Consider a help panel that begins hidden by a CSS class. HTML gives the panel a meaningful heading and a real button. CSS controls the panel's visual state. JavaScript can attach behavior so activating the button changes the state that CSS presents. The code should not replace a meaningful button with a nonsemantic imitation merely to make scripting convenient. It should also avoid embedding a growing collection of inline handlers into markup when a separate script can manage behavior. The result is easier to inspect: HTML explains what exists, CSS explains how it appears, and JavaScript explains what changes and when.

vocabulary.definition: A programming language commonly executed in browsers to implement behavior on web pages and also used in other environments.
Running on the user's device, such as in a browser, rather than on the web server.
The host context that runs code and provides the facilities available to it.
An interface supplied by a browser that code can use to request a browser capability.
The Document Object Model: a browser API representation of a document that scripts can inspect and change.
A program or program source associated with a web document for execution.
A script processed as a JavaScript module; in HTML, module scripts are deferred by default.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Imagine a school play. HTML is the script that says which people, props, and scenes exist. CSS is the costume and lighting plan that says how those things look. JavaScript is the stage manager's set of instructions for what should happen while the play is running: when a curtain opens, when a sign changes, or what happens after someone presses a button.

The stage manager works inside the theater. In the same way, JavaScript in a browser works inside a browser tab. The browser gives it tools, such as a way to look at and update the page. Those tools are browser APIs. JavaScript is the language used to give instructions; the browser API is a tool the browser makes available. The same language can be used in a different place, such as a server, where the available tools are different.
eli10.analogy: HTML is a play's script, CSS is its visual design plan, and JavaScript is the stage manager's runtime instructions.
eli10.analogyLimits: A stage manager is a person with broad real-world judgment, whereas JavaScript follows exact program instructions and browser rules. The analogy also does not explain how code is written or how browser APIs are specified.

workedExample: A museum page has a real HTML button labeled “Show exhibit hours” and a paragraph containing the hours. CSS initially presents that paragraph as hidden. The page needs the paragraph to appear when a visitor activates the button. HTML supplies the button and the information, CSS supplies the hidden and visible presentation, and JavaScript supplies the behavior that changes the relevant state after activation. If the button label is inaccurate, edit HTML; if the panel uses unreadable colors, edit CSS; if activation produces no change, investigate the JavaScript-to-browser-API behavior path. The example deliberately stops before teaching the syntax for selecting elements or listening for events, which belong to later lessons.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating JavaScript as a replacement for meaningful HTML.
commonMistakes.correction: Use suitable HTML for content and semantics, then add JavaScript behavior where it is needed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the DOM as another name for the JavaScript language.
commonMistakes.correction: JavaScript is the language; the DOM is a browser API that JavaScript can use.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming JavaScript always runs in a browser.
commonMistakes.correction: JavaScript has browser and non-browser environments; identify the host when reasoning about available capabilities.

commonMistakes.mistake: Changing CSS when the requirement is an interaction or state change.
commonMistakes.correction: Use CSS for presentation and JavaScript for behavior, while recognizing that a feature can involve both.

compareContrast.distinction: HTML represents content and structure; JavaScript can implement runtime behavior for a page.
CSS describes presentation; JavaScript can decide or trigger changes in response to runtime conditions.
JavaScript is the programming language; a browser API is a host-provided interface usable from JavaScript.
Client-side code runs in a user's browser; server-side code runs on server infrastructure and has a different host environment.

keyTakeaway: JavaScript commonly provides web-page behavior in a browser. It works with, rather than replaces, HTML structure and CSS presentation, and it uses browser APIs within the browser's execution environment.

questionBank.prompt: What is JavaScript commonly used for in a browser-based web page?
options: Defining the page's heading hierarchy
Adding runtime behavior and dynamic updates
Choosing only font families and colors
Registering a domain name
questionBank.explanation: JavaScript commonly implements behavior and dynamic updates. HTML provides structure, CSS handles presentation, and domain registration is an infrastructure task.

questionBank.prompt: Which pairing correctly matches a web technology to its primary introductory role?
options: HTML—runtime behavior; CSS—server database; JavaScript—document headings
HTML—content and structure; CSS—presentation; JavaScript—behavior
HTML—browser API; CSS—programming language host; JavaScript—markup
HTML—domain lookup; CSS—encryption; JavaScript—file hosting
questionBank.explanation: The second pairing captures the standard division of introductory web roles. The other pairings confuse the technologies with infrastructure or APIs.

questionBank.prompt: A developer says, “The DOM is JavaScript.” What is the more accurate correction?
options: The DOM is a CSS feature that JavaScript cannot use.
The DOM is a server-only database.
The DOM is a browser-provided API that JavaScript can use to work with a document.
The DOM is the name for a module script's file extension.
questionBank.explanation: The DOM is a browser API, not the JavaScript language. JavaScript running in a browser can use it to work with a page; the other descriptions are incorrect.

questionBank.prompt: A page has accurate HTML and an attractive CSS layout, but activating “Show details” should reveal an existing panel and does nothing. Which layer should be investigated first?
options: JavaScript behavior associated with the activation
The document's heading wording
The page's font-size declaration only
The site's domain registration
questionBank.explanation: The unmet requirement is behavior after activation, so JavaScript is the appropriate first layer to investigate. HTML wording, CSS font size, and domain registration do not directly provide that behavior.
questionBank.skill: Choose a layer based on a runtime requirement

questionBank.prompt: Why does a script's loading timing matter when it will work with page elements?
options: It changes the semantic meaning of every HTML element.
It guarantees that CSS color choices meet accessibility requirements.
It lets one browser tab read all data from other tabs.
The code may need the relevant HTML to have been parsed before it uses those elements.
questionBank.explanation: A script that works with page elements may depend on the relevant HTML having been parsed. Timing does not alter semantics, guarantee colors, or remove browser isolation.
questionBank.skill: Reason about script timing and document availability

options: Defining the page's heading hierarchy

Registering a domain name
quickCheck.explanation: JavaScript commonly implements behavior and dynamic updates. HTML provides structure, CSS handles presentation, and domain registration is an infrastructure task.

HTML—browser API; CSS—programming language host; JavaScript—markup
HTML—domain lookup; CSS—encryption; JavaScript—file hosting
quickCheck.explanation: The second pairing captures the standard division of introductory web roles. The other pairings confuse the technologies with infrastructure or APIs.

options: The DOM is a CSS feature that JavaScript cannot use.
The DOM is a server-only database.
The DOM is a browser-provided API that JavaScript can use to work with a document.
The DOM is the name for a module script's file extension.
quickCheck.explanation: The DOM is a browser API, not the JavaScript language. JavaScript running in a browser can use it to work with a page; the other descriptions are incorrect.

title: JavaScript Fundamentals
in30Seconds: JavaScript source code is made from pieces that produce values and pieces that tell the engine to do something. An expression, such as `2 + 3`, evaluates to a value. A statement, such as an expression followed by a semicolon, is an instruction in the program. Values have types: familiar primitive examples include strings, numbers, booleans, `null`, and `undefined`. Learning to identify these roles makes short programs easier to read and debug.
whyItMatters: JavaScript is the programming language commonly used to add behavior to web pages, but its fundamentals matter before browser-specific work begins. Reading expressions and statements accurately helps a student predict what code will evaluate to, recognize a type mismatch, and locate an error without guessing. These concepts also transfer to later topics: variables give names to values, functions combine statements into reusable behavior, and browser APIs use the same expression-and-value model. This lesson stays deliberately below those later layers.
learningObjectives: Define a JavaScript value, expression, and statement.
Identify common primitive value types.
Distinguish evaluation from an instruction that performs an action.
Apply arithmetic and comparison operators to predict simple results.

collegeVersion.heading: Values and their types
collegeVersion.body:
A value is a piece of data that JavaScript can work with. The language has several primitive value types: `undefined`, `null`, Boolean, Number, BigInt, String, and Symbol. A primitive is a value that is not an object. At an introductory level, the most visible examples are numbers such as `12`, strings such as `"hello"`, Booleans `true` and `false`, and the special values `null` and `undefined`. These labels are not interchangeable. A number is suitable for arithmetic; a string represents text; a Boolean represents one of two logical states. `null` is an explicit primitive value often used to represent an intentional absence, whereas `undefined` is its own primitive value and commonly appears when no value has been supplied. Later lessons explain how names, collections, and objects hold or organize values; this lesson concentrates on the values themselves.

Type matters because an operator's behavior depends on its operands. `2 + 3` is numeric addition and produces the Number value `5`. The comparison `2 < 3` produces the Boolean value `true`. A careful reader therefore asks both questions: what values are present, and what type of result should this operation produce? That habit is more reliable than reading punctuation as decoration. JavaScript can perform conversions in some situations, but relying on an unexamined conversion makes code harder to reason about. When a result surprises you, inspect the values and their types first.

collegeVersion.heading: Expressions evaluate
collegeVersion.body:
An expression is code that resolves to a value. A literal such as `"Ada"` is an expression: evaluating it yields that string. An arithmetic expression such as `6 * 7` evaluates to `42`. Expressions can be combined. In `2 + 3 * 4`, multiplication is evaluated before addition, so the resulting Number value is `14`, not `20`. Parentheses can deliberately change that grouping: `(2 + 3) * 4` evaluates to `20`. Executing these examples in a JavaScript runtime confirms the results.

Operators are symbols or keywords that participate in expressions. Arithmetic operators include `+`, `-`, `*`, and `/`. Comparison operators, including `===`, `<`, and `>`, evaluate whether a relationship is true and yield a Boolean result. `5 === 5` evaluates to `true`; `5 === 6` evaluates to `false`. The strict equality operator compares without first converting the operands to a common type, which makes its result easier to predict than a loose equality check in many introductory cases. This lesson does not attempt to catalog every operator. The central model is that operators receive operands and an expression evaluates to one resulting value.

A result need not be displayed merely because an expression has a value. Interactive developer consoles often show the result of an entered expression as a convenience. That display is a feature of the host environment, not an implication that every expression automatically appears on a web page. Separating JavaScript language evaluation from browser output prevents a common early misunderstanding.

collegeVersion.heading: Statements organize actions
collegeVersion.body:
A statement is a complete instruction in a program. ECMAScript source text contains statements, and an expression statement is one familiar form: it evaluates an expression as an instruction. In many JavaScript examples, a semicolon marks the end of a statement. JavaScript has automatic semicolon insertion rules, but beginners should not treat omitted punctuation as a separate feature to depend on; clear formatting makes statement boundaries easier for humans to see. A program generally contains a sequence of statements, with each statement contributing to the program's behavior.

The expression/statement distinction is about role, not about which one is more advanced. `3 * 5` is an expression because it yields `15`. Written as a standalone expression statement, it instructs the engine to evaluate that expression, though the completion value is not thereby made useful to a person. By contrast, a comment is not an instruction for the engine at all. JavaScript comments—`//` to the end of a line and `/* ... */` across text—are ignored by the engine. They can record intent for future readers, but a comment cannot alter an evaluated result.

This vocabulary helps with debugging. If an expected result is wrong, inspect the expression: its operands, operator, precedence, and types. If intended work never occurs, inspect whether the necessary statement exists and is reached; control flow is a later topic. If only a comment describes an intended action, the engine will not carry it out. These distinctions remain useful as code becomes more complex, even though later lessons add variables, functions, arrays, objects, and web APIs.

vocabulary.definition: A piece of data produced, represented, or used by JavaScript code.
A JavaScript value that is not an object, such as a string, number, Boolean, null, or undefined.
A unit of JavaScript code that evaluates to a value.
A complete JavaScript instruction in program source text.
A symbol or keyword used in an expression to act on one or more operands.
A value or expression to which an operator is applied.
The JavaScript primitive type with the two values true and false.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Imagine JavaScript as a tiny workshop. Values are the materials on the table: a number, a piece of text, or a yes/no card. An expression is a small calculation card. When the workshop reads `2 + 3`, it works with two number materials and produces a new material, `5`. A comparison card such as `2 < 3` produces a yes/no card: `true`.

A statement is closer to an instruction posted for the workshop: do this piece of work now. It can contain an expression, but the two words answer different questions. Ask “what value comes out?” for an expression and “what instruction is this?” for a statement. A comment is a sticky note for another person, not an instruction the workshop follows.
eli10.analogy: Values are workshop materials, expressions are calculation cards that make a result, and statements are posted work instructions.
eli10.analogyLimits: Real JavaScript is formal language processing, not a person choosing materials. The analogy does not cover execution order, browser APIs, or how later code stores values.

workedExample: Run these expressions in a JavaScript console: `2 + 3 * 4` evaluates to `14`, because multiplication groups before addition. `(2 + 3) * 4` evaluates to `20`, because the parentheses change the grouping. Next, `14 === 20` evaluates to the Boolean `false`; it compares two Number values and finds they differ. The first two snippets are arithmetic expressions that produce Number values. The third is a comparison expression that produces a Boolean. If each is entered as a standalone line, the console may show its result, but that display is the console helping the reader. A line comment such as `// compare the two totals` explains the next line to a human and has no evaluated value or effect on the calculation.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling every line of code an expression.
commonMistakes.correction: Ask whether the code's role is to produce a value; if it is a complete instruction, call it a statement.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting a comparison to produce a number.
commonMistakes.correction: Comparison operators such as `<` and `===` produce Boolean results.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a console result is automatically page output.
commonMistakes.correction: A console may display evaluated values for convenience; displaying content in a page needs later browser APIs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating `null` and `undefined` as the same value.
commonMistakes.correction: They are distinct JavaScript primitive values, even though both can arise in absence-related situations.

compareContrast.distinction: An expression evaluates to a value; a statement is a program instruction and may contain expressions.
A number represents numeric data; a Boolean is either true or false.
A comment assists human readers and is ignored by the engine; a statement is processed as program source.

keyTakeaway: Values have types, expressions evaluate to values, and statements organize program instructions. Naming the role of each piece of code makes JavaScript behavior more predictable.

questionBank.prompt: Which JavaScript expression evaluates to a Boolean value?
options: `null`
questionBank.explanation: `4 > 1` is a comparison and evaluates to `true`, a Boolean. The others evaluate to a number, a string, and null respectively.
questionBank.skill: Identify the result type of a comparison expression

questionBank.prompt: What does `(2 + 3) * 4` evaluate to?
questionBank.explanation: Parentheses make `2 + 3` evaluate first to 5; 5 multiplied by 4 is 20. The other values come from different or incorrect groupings.

questionBank.prompt: Which description best distinguishes an expression from a statement?
options: An expression evaluates to a value; a statement is a program instruction.
An expression is only text; a statement is only a number.
An expression runs only in browsers; a statement runs only on servers.
An expression is a comment; a statement is punctuation.
questionBank.explanation: The first option states the roles accurately. Expressions are not limited by host environment, and comments are ignored by the engine.

questionBank.prompt: A developer writes `// calculate total` above an arithmetic expression. What does the comment do?
options: It changes the expression into a string.
It forces the result to appear on the page.
It makes the expression evaluate twice.
It explains intent to readers while the engine ignores it.
questionBank.explanation: A comment can guide a human reader but is ignored by the JavaScript engine. It does not change evaluation or page output.

JavaScript cannot compare numbers.

title: Variables
in30Seconds: In JavaScript, a variable is commonly introduced with `let` or `const`. Each declaration creates a named binding: a name the program can use to refer to a value. Use `let` when the binding will later be assigned a different value. Use `const` when the binding itself should not be reassigned after initialization. Both are block-scoped, so a name declared inside braces is available only within that block and nested blocks.
whyItMatters: Variables give a program a way to keep track of changing information without losing the meaning of each value. The `let`/`const` distinction also makes an intention visible to a reader: is this name expected to change, or should a later assignment be treated as a mistake? Block scope prevents temporary names from leaking into unrelated code. These habits make small scripts easier to debug and scale into later JavaScript work, where data moves through functions, browser events, and page updates.
learningObjectives: Define a JavaScript binding and distinguish declaration from initialization.
Choose `let` or `const` for a simple binding based on reassignment intent.
Explain why a `const` binding cannot receive a new assignment.
Trace the visibility of a `let` or `const` name across nested blocks.
Identify a temporal-dead-zone error caused by using a lexical binding too early.

collegeVersion.heading: Names bind to values
collegeVersion.body: JavaScript code needs a way to associate a meaningful name with a value. In this lesson, that association is called a binding. A declaration introduces the name; an initializer supplies its first value when one is present. For example, `const campus = "North";` declares the binding `campus` and initializes it with a string value in one statement. `let visits;` declares a binding without giving it an initial value; JavaScript initially gives that binding the value `undefined`, and a later assignment such as `visits = 1;` changes it. The terms matter because declaration, initialization, and assignment are different operations. A program can assign to an already declared `let` binding, but it cannot declare the same `let` name twice in the same scope. Precise vocabulary makes error messages easier to interpret and helps a reader see what a line is intended to do. This lesson discusses bindings, not a physical storage box: the useful model is the language rule that a name refers to a value in a particular scope.

collegeVersion.heading: Choosing let or const
collegeVersion.body: `let` and `const` are lexical declarations. For an introductory rule, choose `const` when a binding will keep the same assignment, and choose `let` when the program will later give that binding another value. For example, a score that changes after a correct answer can be introduced with `let score = 0;` and later updated with `score = score + 1;`. A label that the program does not reassign can use `const label = "Practice";`. A `const` declaration must have an initializer, so `const label;` is an error. Once a const binding is initialized, attempting `label = "Quiz";` is also an error. This rule concerns the binding, not a broad promise that every value associated with it is permanently unchanged; later lessons on objects and arrays introduce a separate distinction about changing properties or elements. Here, keep the question narrow: will this name receive a new assignment? If yes, use `let`; if no, `const` communicates that plan and lets JavaScript reject an accidental reassignment.

collegeVersion.heading: Block scope controls where a name works
collegeVersion.body: A block is code surrounded by braces, as in `{ ... }`. Bindings declared with `let` and `const` are block-scoped. A binding introduced inside a block can be used in that block and in blocks nested within it, but not after the block closes. This supports local reasoning. A short-lived calculation can have a temporary name without risking a collision with code after the block. Consider `let message = "outside"; { let message = "inside"; }`. The second declaration creates a distinct inner binding. While execution is inside the braces, `message` names the inner value; after the braces, it names the outer value again. This is shadowing: an inner name temporarily hides an outer binding with the same spelling. Shadowing is legal in nested scopes but can make code harder to read, so use it intentionally and favor descriptive names when the relationship is not obvious. A binding declared within the braces does not become available outside them merely because code in the block ran.

collegeVersion.heading: Declaration order and the temporal dead zone
collegeVersion.body: Lexical scope is not permission to use a binding before its declaration has been evaluated. Within the scope of a `let` or `const` declaration, the name is in a temporal dead zone from the start of that scope until the declaration executes. Reading the name during that interval throws a `ReferenceError`. For example, `{ console.log(total); let total = 4; }` does not print `undefined`; it fails before the declaration initializes `total`. Put declarations before code that reads them. This ordering rule is one reason `let` and `const` avoid a class of confusing behavior associated with older declaration patterns. It also gives a practical debugging checklist: if a name is reported as unavailable even though a declaration appears later in the same block, look for a use above the declaration. The temporal-dead-zone idea does not mean the name is invisible forever. It means the block has begun to reserve that name, but the binding is not ready for access until its declaration has run.

vocabulary.definition: The association a program creates between an identifier and a value in a particular scope.
A statement that introduces a binding name, such as one beginning with `let` or `const`.
The expression that provides a declared binding's first value.
An operation that gives a new value to an existing assignable binding.
An assignment that replaces the value previously associated with a binding.
Visibility limited to a brace-delimited block and any blocks nested inside it.
A nested declaration using the same name as an outer binding, so the inner binding is selected within its scope.
The interval after a lexical scope begins but before a particular `let` or `const` declaration is evaluated, when that binding cannot be accessed.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: A variable name is like a label a program uses when it needs to find a value again. `let` is a label the program plans to replace later, such as a score that starts at zero and then goes up. `const` is a label the program promises not to replace, such as the title chosen for a page. Both kinds of labels follow the room made by curly braces. A label made inside one room is not on the table outside that room. If there is a smaller room inside, it can use a label with the same spelling, but while you are in the smaller room, that inner label is the one you see.
eli10.analogy: Imagine color-coded sticky notes on folders. A `let` note can be moved to another folder later. A `const` note is attached with a rule that says it cannot be moved to a different folder. Curly braces make a temporary work area: sticky notes placed inside are usable there but are removed from the shared desk when the work area closes. A smaller work area can use a note with the same word, temporarily covering the view of the older one.
eli10.analogyLimits: JavaScript bindings are language-defined relationships, not physical notes. In particular, the analogy should not suggest that `const` makes every possible aspect of a value immutable; this lesson only establishes that the binding cannot be reassigned. JavaScript also enforces scope and early access rules mechanically, whereas people can read a sticky note before a meeting starts.

workedExample: Run this JavaScript in order: `let score = 0; score = score + 1; const course = "Web Basics"; { let score = 10; console.log(score); } console.log(score); console.log(course);`. The first assignment changes the outer `score` from `0` to `1`, which is permitted because it was declared with `let`. The block then declares a separate inner `score` with value `10`; the first log prints `10`. When the block ends, that inner binding is no longer selected, so the next log prints the unchanged outer value `1`. The final log prints `Web Basics`. Replacing the final `course` use with `course = "Advanced Web";` would throw because a const binding cannot be reassigned. The example was executed with Bun: its output was `10`, `1`, and `Web Basics` on separate lines.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using `const` for a name that the program will deliberately update.
commonMistakes.correction: Use `let` when a later assignment is part of the design; otherwise the later assignment will fail.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking `let` and `const` names declared inside braces exist after the closing brace.
commonMistakes.correction: Treat the block as the boundary: a lexical binding is usable in its block and nested blocks, not outside it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting a `let` or `const` name used before its declaration to behave as if it were initialized to `undefined`.
commonMistakes.correction: Put the declaration before the first use; early access is a temporal-dead-zone `ReferenceError`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the inner and outer uses of the same name are automatically one binding.
commonMistakes.correction: A nested declaration creates an inner binding that shadows the outer one only within the nested block.

compareContrast.distinction: A let binding may receive a new assignment; a const binding must be initialized and may not be reassigned.
A declaration introduces a binding name, while an assignment gives a value to an already existing assignable binding.
The outer binding is selected outside the nested block; the inner binding with the same name is selected while execution is inside its own block.

keyTakeaway: Use `let` for a binding that will be reassigned and `const` for one that will not. Both are block-scoped, so declare names before using them and keep track of the braces that define where each name is available.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement correctly describes a `const` declaration?
options: It must include an initializer and its binding cannot later be reassigned.
It can be declared without a value and assigned only outside a block.
It is visible in every script regardless of braces.
It is a special syntax for an array.
questionBank.explanation: A const declaration needs an initializer, and later reassignment of that binding is an error. The other options incorrectly describe initialization, scope, or introduce an unrelated array claim.

questionBank.prompt: Which change is permitted after this declaration: `let count = 2;`?
options: `let count = 3;` in the same scope
`count = 3;`
`const count = 3;` in the same scope
`count` cannot be used again.
questionBank.explanation: `count = 3;` reassigns the existing let binding. Declaring it again with let or const in the same scope is not permitted, and a let binding remains usable after declaration.

questionBank.prompt: What happens when this code runs? `let label = "outer"; { let label = "inner"; } console.log(label);`
options: It throws because two blocks cannot use the same name.
It logs `inner` because the inner binding permanently replaces the outer one.
It logs `outer` because the inner binding exists only inside the braces.
It logs `undefined` because block scope removes both bindings.
questionBank.explanation: The nested declaration creates an inner binding that shadows the outer one only in the block. After the block closes, `label` again selects the outer binding, whose value is `outer`.

questionBank.prompt: Why does `{ console.log(total); const total = 4; }` fail before logging a value?
options: The `console` identifier is allowed only in a function.
Const values must be numeric strings rather than numbers.
The braces turn every declaration into a global binding.

questionBank.explanation: The binding is in its temporal dead zone until the const declaration evaluates, so early access throws a ReferenceError. The other answers do not describe JavaScript's lexical declaration rule.

title: Functions
in30Seconds: A JavaScript function is reusable code that can be called to perform a task or calculate a value. A declaration gives the function a name, optional parameters, and a body. A call supplies arguments for those parameters. When a function uses `return`, the call evaluates to the returned value; without a return statement, an ordinary function call produces `undefined`.
whyItMatters: Functions let a program give one job a clear name and reuse its logic instead of copying it into every place that needs it. That makes a page's behavior easier to test, explain, and change. In later web work, functions organize event handlers, data transformations, and requests, but the same fundamentals still apply: understand what inputs a function expects, what it returns, and which work belongs inside it.
learningObjectives: Define a JavaScript function declaration, call, parameter, and argument.
Distinguish a parameter from an argument.
Explain how `return` determines the value produced by a call.
Apply a small function to calculate and reuse a result.

collegeVersion.heading: Declaration, body, and call
collegeVersion.body:
A function declaration introduces a callable function with the `function` keyword, an identifier, a parenthesized parameter list, and a statement body in braces. For example, `function greet(name) { return `Hello, ${name}!`; }` declares a function named `greet`. Declaring it does not run the body. The body runs when code evaluates a call expression such as `greet("Mina")`. Separating declaration from call is useful: the declaration describes a reusable operation, while each call is one use of that operation. This lesson focuses on ordinary declared functions; arrow functions, methods, callbacks, asynchronous functions, and browser DOM work are separate subjects.

The function body is a block of statements. It can create local values, make decisions, and calculate a result. Good beginner functions tend to have one understandable responsibility, such as formatting a label or computing a total. That is not a rule that every function must be tiny, but it is a practical way to make behavior easier to inspect. A useful name describes the operation—`calculateTotal` says more than `doThing`. Naming also helps a reader identify the intended job at each call site, but a name cannot substitute for checking the body and its returned value.

collegeVersion.heading: Parameters receive arguments
collegeVersion.body:
Parameters are names written in a function's definition. They act as local bindings when a call begins. Arguments are the actual values written at a particular call site. In `function square(number) { return number * number; }`, `number` is a parameter. In `square(5)`, `5` is an argument. The distinction matters because the same declared function can be called with different arguments: `square(2)` and `square(9)` reuse the same body but produce different results.

JavaScript does not require a call to provide the same number of arguments as the declaration has parameters. When no argument is supplied for a parameter, its initial value is `undefined` unless the declaration supplies a default parameter value. Extra arguments do not create additional named parameters in this simple declaration. That flexibility is not a reason to ignore expected inputs. A function's name, parameter names, and documentation should communicate what callers are meant to provide. Keep values that are only needed during one call inside that function unless there is a deliberate reason to share state.

collegeVersion.heading: Return values and observable results
collegeVersion.body:
A `return` statement ends the current function execution and supplies a value to the caller. In `function add(a, b) { return a + b; }`, the expression `add(3, 4)` evaluates to `7`, so another expression can use it: `const total = add(3, 4);`. Returning a value is different from merely displaying one. `console.log(total)` writes a diagnostic message to a console, while `return total` gives the calling code a value it can store, compare, or pass onward.

If execution reaches the end of an ordinary function without a `return` statement, the call's result is `undefined`. A bare `return;` also returns `undefined`. This is often appropriate for a function whose purpose is an effect, but it is a bug when calling code expects a calculation. A return statement can appear before later statements in the same body; those later statements are not reached on that call. That is another reason to keep a function's result logic clear and deliberate. A caller can compose returned values—for example, use one function's result as an argument to another—without the called function knowing who will consume it. Testing a function with representative inputs and comparing the returned value with an expected value can reveal errors before its behavior is connected to any interface. When reading or writing a function, ask three concrete questions: What arguments does it use? What work does it perform? What value, if any, does the caller receive? Those questions make function behavior testable without involving a web page or a network request.

vocabulary.definition: Syntax that creates a named function with a parameter list and a body.
An expression that invokes a function, usually by writing its name followed by parentheses.
A named local binding listed in a function definition for receiving an input.
A value supplied in the parentheses of a particular function call.
A statement that ends the current function execution and optionally supplies a value to its caller.
The JavaScript value commonly produced when a function finishes without returning a value.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Think of a function as a named mini-recipe in a program. You write the recipe once, then call its name whenever you want the program to follow those steps. The empty spots in the recipe are parameters. When you call the function, you put actual ingredients—arguments—into those spots. A `return` is what the recipe hands back when it finishes, such as a finished total or a formatted message. A function can also finish without handing anything back; in JavaScript, that result is `undefined`.
eli10.analogy: A smoothie counter has a recipe called `makeSmoothie(fruit, milk)`. `fruit` and `milk` are the labels on the recipe's blanks (parameters). Saying `makeSmoothie("banana", "oat milk")` provides this order's ingredients (arguments). The finished smoothie is the return value.
eli10.analogyLimits: A program does not have a person or physical ingredients, and a function may do more than calculate one finished object. Also, JavaScript permits calls with missing or extra arguments, unlike a real counter that might reject an incomplete order.

workedExample: Suppose a checkout needs a total including tax. Write `function totalWithTax(price, rate) { const tax = price * rate; return price + tax; }`. Here `price` and `rate` are parameters; `20` and `0.05` are arguments in `totalWithTax(20, 0.05)`. The calculation is `20 * 0.05`, which is `1`, then `20 + 1`, which is `21`. Executing this exact function with Bun printed `21`. Because it returns the result, a caller can store it: `const due = totalWithTax(20, 0.05);`. Replacing `return price + tax` with `console.log(price + tax)` would display 21 but would not make `due` equal to 21.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling a parameter an argument everywhere.
commonMistakes.correction: Use parameter for the name in the declaration and argument for the value in a call.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting a declaration to run immediately.
commonMistakes.correction: A declaration creates the function; a call invokes its body.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using `console.log` when later code needs a computed value.
commonMistakes.correction: Return the value and let the caller decide whether to display it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a function without `return` produces its last computed expression.
commonMistakes.correction: An ordinary JavaScript function that reaches its end without returning produces `undefined`.

compareContrast.distinction: A parameter is named in the function definition; an argument is supplied by one call.
`return` supplies a value to the caller and ends the function; `console.log` displays a value but does not return that displayed value.

keyTakeaway: A function declaration defines reusable behavior. Calls provide arguments for parameters, and `return` determines the value a caller can use afterward.

questionBank.prompt: In `function square(number) { return number * number; }`, what is `number`?
options: An argument
A return value
A parameter
A function call

questionBank.explanation: Different calls can supply different argument values to the same parameterized body. The other changes do not provide reusable input-driven calculation.

title: Arrays
in30Seconds: A JavaScript array is an ordered collection whose elements are accessed with numeric indexes. The first position is index `0`, and the `length` property reports one more than the greatest present index. Bracket notation reads or assigns an element, while methods such as `push()`, `pop()`, `shift()`, and `unshift()` add or remove elements. Many common array operations change the same array, so track that mutation deliberately.
whyItMatters: Arrays give JavaScript programs a compact way to keep related values in an order: tasks in a queue, test scores, or items a page should render. Indexing makes it possible to select one item, while the length makes bounds checks and loops possible. The essential habit is distinguishing a method that changes an existing array from one that creates a result without changing it. That distinction prevents surprising data changes in browser interfaces and is a foundation for later work with loops, DOM updates, and API data.
learningObjectives: Define a JavaScript array and identify its zero-based indexes.
Use bracket notation to read or assign an array element.
Explain what an array's length represents.
Trace the effects of basic methods that add or remove elements.
Distinguish mutation of an array from reassignment of its variable binding.

collegeVersion.heading: Ordered elements and indexes
collegeVersion.body: An array is an object-like JavaScript collection designed around ordered element positions. An array literal uses square brackets: `const colors = ["red", "blue", "green"];`. Its elements occupy numeric indexes. JavaScript begins indexing at zero, so `colors[0]` is `"red"`, `colors[1]` is `"blue"`, and `colors[2]` is `"green"`. The bracket expression is not a one-based human counting system; it asks for the element associated with a property key representing an array index. That is why asking for `colors[3]` in this example returns `undefined`: no element has been stored at that position. Zero-based indexing can initially feel off by one, but it gives a direct relationship between an index and its offset from the start: index 0 is zero positions away, index 1 is one position away. Keep this lesson focused on ordered elements; named properties belong to the separate topic on objects.

collegeVersion.heading: Length is a boundary, not the last index
collegeVersion.body: Every array has a `length` property. For `const colors = ["red", "blue", "green"];`, `colors.length` is `3`. The last existing element is therefore at `colors.length - 1`, or index 2. A frequent error is to use `colors[colors.length]` when trying to retrieve the last element; that expression instead asks for the first position after the normal end and returns `undefined` here. Array length is maintained from indexed elements, and it can describe a range that includes empty positions. For introductory code, the safe model is that valid existing positions in a dense array run from 0 through `length - 1`. Check the boundary before reading a position when input might be empty. An empty array `[]` has length 0 and no last element, so `items[items.length - 1]` is not a useful element lookup until the program has established that `items.length > 0`.

collegeVersion.heading: Reading, assigning, and changing the collection
collegeVersion.body: Bracket notation can read an element or assign an element at an index. Given `const tasks = ["plan", "draft"];`, `tasks[1]` reads `"draft"`; `tasks[1] = "review"` replaces that element. Arrays also provide methods for common end and front operations. `push(value)` appends one or more values and returns the new length. `pop()` removes and returns the final element. `unshift(value)` adds one or more values at the beginning and returns the new length; `shift()` removes and returns the first element. These methods mutate the target array. Mutation means the collection itself changes, so another part of a program observing the same array will observe the updated elements. By contrast, `slice()` returns a new array containing a selected portion and does not mutate the source. Knowing which category a method belongs to is more useful than memorizing a long method list: inspect the documentation and make the intended data change explicit.

collegeVersion.heading: Mutation is not reassignment
collegeVersion.body: An array can be held by a `const` binding and still have elements changed. `const list = ["a"]; list.push("b");` is permitted because `push()` mutates the array rather than assigning a different value to the binding `list`. In contrast, `list = ["a", "b"];` attempts to reassign that const binding and throws. The difference matters when reading code: `const` protects the association between the name and the array, not the array's contents. When an operation should preserve the original array, use a non-mutating operation such as `slice()` and store its result under an appropriate binding. This is also a design choice: a function that silently mutates input can surprise a caller, while a clearly named operation and a documented returned array make ownership easier to reason about. For values arriving from an unknown source, `Array.isArray(value)` tests whether the value is an array; do not rely only on a value's appearance in console output. This lesson does not treat arrays as a substitute for keyed records, nested data structures, functions, or browser APIs; those choices require different concepts.

vocabulary.definition: A JavaScript collection that stores elements at ordered numeric index positions.
A value stored in an array at a particular index.
A zero-based numeric position used to access an array element.
An array property giving the boundary one position beyond its highest normal indexed element.
The `[index]` syntax used to read or assign an element at an array position.
A change made to an existing collection rather than a replacement of the variable binding that refers to it.
To add an element after the current final position of an array.
An array whose positions from zero through length minus one each hold an element.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: An array is a numbered row of slots for related things. JavaScript starts the slot numbers at zero, so the first song in a playlist is in slot 0. The array's length tells you how many slots are in use, but it is not itself the number of the last slot. You can replace something in a slot, add a thing at the end with `push`, or remove the last thing with `pop`. Those actions change the same row of slots.
eli10.analogy: Imagine a tray of numbered cubbies. The first cubby says 0, the next says 1, and so on. `push` puts a new item in the next cubby at the end; `pop` takes the item from the final cubby. The tray's length is the number of cubbies currently counted, so the last item's cubby number is one less than that count.
eli10.analogyLimits: JavaScript arrays are not fixed physical trays. Their length can change, and they can even have missing positions, so a real tray is only a guide to indexing and order. The analogy also cannot tell you whether an operation mutates an array; that comes from JavaScript's method rules.

workedExample: Execute: `const tasks = ["plan", "draft", "review"]; tasks.push("publish"); const first = tasks.shift(); const last = tasks.pop(); console.log(JSON.stringify(tasks), tasks.length, first, last);`. Start with three elements at indexes 0–2. `push` appends `publish`, so the array becomes four elements. `shift` removes and returns the first element, `plan`, leaving `["draft", "review", "publish"]`. `pop` then removes and returns `publish`, leaving `["draft", "review"]`. The remaining array has length 2, with elements at indexes 0 and 1. Run with Bun, the output is `["draft","review"] 2 plan publish`. The original `tasks` array changed at each method call; no reassignment was needed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating index 1 as the first array position.
commonMistakes.correction: JavaScript arrays are zero-indexed, so the first element is at index 0.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using `array[array.length]` for the last element.
commonMistakes.correction: For a nonempty dense array, the last element is at `array[array.length - 1]`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting `push`, `pop`, `shift`, or `unshift` to leave the original array unchanged.
commonMistakes.correction: These methods mutate their target array; use a documented non-mutating operation when preservation is required.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming `const` prevents changes to elements.
commonMistakes.correction: Const prevents reassignment of the binding, not mutation of the array stored through that binding.

compareContrast.distinction: An index selects a position starting at zero; length is the boundary one past the final normal position.
Push appends and returns a new length; pop removes and returns the final element.
Mutation changes elements in an existing array; reassignment makes a binding refer to a different value.

keyTakeaway: Use arrays for ordered values, count from index 0, and treat `length` as the boundary after the final element. Before calling an array method, know whether it changes the original array and what it returns.

title: Objects
in30Seconds: A JavaScript object groups related information as properties. Each property connects a key to a value, such as a course object's `title` and `seats`. An object literal uses braces: `const course = { title: "Web Basics", seats: 24 };`. Use dot notation when you know a simple property name, and bracket notation when the key comes from a variable or is not a valid identifier. Assigning to a property can add it or replace its value.
whyItMatters: Objects give web programs a readable way to keep related facts together. A product, a user preference, or a page setting can be represented by one object rather than a collection of unrelated variables. Learning exactly how keys are read and changed prevents common bugs, especially when a program chooses a property name at runtime. This foundation leads into browser APIs and DOM work, but the immediate skill is smaller: represent a record of related data, read the needed value, and update the intended property.
learningObjectives: Define an object, property, key, and value in JavaScript.
Create a plain object with an object literal.
Read a known property with dot notation.
Use bracket notation for a computed or non-identifier key.
Trace an assignment that adds or replaces an object property.

collegeVersion.heading: An object is a collection of named properties
collegeVersion.body: In JavaScript, an object is a value that can have properties. A property associates a key (also called a property name) with a value. That value may be a string, number, boolean, another object, or a function; this lesson uses ordinary data values so the structure stays visible. An object literal is a direct expression for creating an object. In `const course = { title: "Web Basics", seats: 24 };`, the braces create one object. `title` and `seats` are keys, while `"Web Basics"` and `24` are their values. The variable `course` holds a reference to that object. Grouping these facts says that they describe the same course. It does not impose a fixed record layout: JavaScript objects can receive new properties later. That flexibility is useful, but it also means a reader must pay attention to the exact spelling of each key. Property names are case-sensitive, so `course.title` and `course.Title` ask for different names. This lesson concerns plain objects used as records, not classes, JSON text, or browser network data.

collegeVersion.heading: Reading properties: dot notation and brackets
collegeVersion.body: Property access has two common forms. Dot notation places an identifier directly after a dot: `course.title`. It is concise when the program literally knows the simple name `title`. Bracket notation puts an expression in square brackets: `course["title"]`. With that string, it reads the same property. Brackets are required when a key has characters that cannot appear in an identifier, such as `course["meeting day"]`, and when the key is held in a variable. For example, `const field = "seats"; course[field]` reads `24`; `course.field` instead looks for a property literally named `field`. This distinction is central: brackets evaluate the expression inside them, while dot notation treats the characters after the dot as the property name. A request for a property that the object does not have normally produces `undefined`, which is different from `null`. Do not treat a missing property as proof that an object is broken; first check the intended key and whether the program was expected to add that property.

collegeVersion.heading: Adding and replacing a property
collegeVersion.body: An assignment through a property access changes the object. `course.seats = 30;` replaces the old value for the existing `seats` property. `course.room = "Lab 3";` adds a new property because no `room` property existed. The same rule applies with brackets: `course[field] = 30;` changes whichever property name the expression in `field` evaluates to. This is separate from reassigning the variable. `const course` means the binding `course` cannot be assigned to a different object, but it does not freeze the object it already refers to. Therefore `course.seats = 30` can work while `course = { title: "Other" }` throws a reassignment error. When code updates data, identify what is changing: the binding, or one property of the referenced object. Use carefully controlled keys for bracket access. This lesson does not cover accepting arbitrary external keys; later security work addresses trust boundaries.

collegeVersion.heading: Trace a small record deliberately
collegeVersion.body: Consider `const schedule = { day: "Tuesday", start: 9 }; const chosen = "start"; schedule[chosen] = schedule[chosen] + 1; schedule.room = "204";`. The literal first creates properties `day` and `start`. `chosen` stores the string `"start"`. Each occurrence of `schedule[chosen]` therefore accesses `schedule.start`, first reading `9` and then writing `10`. The final line adds `room`. At the end, the object represents `{ day: "Tuesday", start: 10, room: "204" }`. This style of tracing is more reliable than guessing from punctuation: write the key selected by every bracket expression, then mark whether an assignment replaces an existing property or creates one. If the code used `schedule.chosen`, it would refer to a different, literal key named `chosen`. Objects are often passed between functions or connected to page elements later, but the access rules do not change: a property read needs the intended key, and an assignment acts on that selected property.

vocabulary.definition: A JavaScript value that can hold properties.
A named association between a key and a value on an object.
The property name used to select a value from an object.
The data currently associated with a property key.
A brace-delimited JavaScript expression that creates an object with listed properties.
Property access written with a dot and a literal identifier, such as `book.title`.
Property access written with square brackets containing an expression, such as `book[field]`.
Selecting a property by evaluating an expression to obtain its key.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Think of an object as one labeled information card. The card for a class can have a line called `title` and another called `seats`. Instead of keeping those facts in separate piles, the object keeps them together. A dot is a quick way to point at a line whose name you already know: `course.title`. Square brackets are useful when someone hands you the line name in another note: if `field` says `"seats"`, then `course[field]` means the seats line. You can erase and replace the value on a line, or add a new line.
eli10.analogy: Imagine a campus directory card. The headings on the card are keys, and the entries written beside them are values. Saying `card.phone` is like pointing at the printed Phone heading. Saying `card[heading]` is like reading a small note that tells you which heading to use, then pointing there.
eli10.analogyLimits: A JavaScript object is not a paper card: values can be other objects or functions, and JavaScript applies formal access rules. The card image also should not suggest that `const` makes the entries unchangeable; it only prevents replacing the variable's reference to the card.

workedExample: Run `const schedule = { day: "Tuesday", start: 9 }; const field = "start"; schedule[field] = schedule[field] + 1; schedule.room = "204"; console.log(schedule.start, schedule["room"]);`. `field` evaluates to `"start"`, so the bracket reads 9 and writes 10 back to the `start` property. The last assignment adds `room`; it does not replace the `schedule` variable. The output is `10 204`. In contrast, `schedule.field` would seek a property literally named `field`, which was never added, so it would be `undefined`. This example was executed with Bun.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing `object.variableName` when a variable holds the desired key.
commonMistakes.correction: Use `object[variableName]`; dot notation would use the literal word `variableName`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using dot notation for a key that contains a space or hyphen.
commonMistakes.correction: Use bracket notation with the exact string key, such as `record["meeting-day"]`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming `const` prevents all changes to an object's properties.
commonMistakes.correction: Distinguish rebinding the variable from assigning to a property of the existing object.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a missing-property result as `null`.
commonMistakes.correction: A normal read of an absent property yields `undefined`; verify the key spelling and creation path.

compareContrast.distinction: Dot notation names a literal identifier; bracket notation evaluates an expression to determine the key.
Reassignment changes what a variable refers to; property assignment changes or adds data on the currently referenced object.

keyTakeaway: Objects organize related data as key–value properties. Use dots for known simple keys, brackets for computed or unusual keys, and trace assignments to see exactly which property changes.
