title: The Document Object Model (DOM)
in30Seconds: The Document Object Model, usually called the DOM, is the browser's in-memory object representation of a document such as an HTML page. It organizes the page as a tree: the document contains elements, and elements can contain other elements and text. JavaScript can locate nodes in that tree, read them, change them, or create and attach new ones. The DOM is a browser-provided API, not a feature built into JavaScript itself.
whyItMatters: The DOM is the bridge between a static HTML document and a page whose visible content can change after it loads. In coursework, it makes document structure, tree relationships, and APIs concrete. In practice, DOM work supports things such as updating a counter, showing a validation message, or rendering a list from data. Knowing what the DOM represents also helps you choose a narrowly targeted selector and avoid accidentally replacing more of a page than intended.
learningObjectives: Define the DOM as a document representation exposed to scripts.
Identify parent, child, element, and text-node relationships in a DOM tree.
Use querySelector() to locate the first element matching a CSS selector.
Explain the difference between changing textContent and inserting HTML markup.
Apply a small, safe DOM update to a known element.

collegeVersion.heading: A document becomes a tree of objects
collegeVersion.body: HTML is sent or loaded as text, but the browser builds a document model it can render and expose to programs. MDN describes the DOM as the representation in memory that connects a document's structure to a script or programming language. In a typical HTML document, the document is the root; html contains head and body; body may contain main, headings, paragraphs, and lists. That containment is why DOM diagrams are commonly drawn as trees. A node can have children, and a child has a parent. An element node corresponds to an element such as a p or button, while text inside an element is represented as text content. The DOM is not the original source file and is not JavaScript syntax. It is an API supplied by the browser, which JavaScript can call. This distinction matters when reading code: document is a browser object, whereas JavaScript supplies the language constructs used to work with it.

collegeVersion.heading: Finding a specific node
collegeVersion.body: Most DOM work begins by getting a reference to an existing node. document.querySelector(selector) accepts a CSS selector and returns the first element in document order that matches it; if nothing matches, it returns null. For example, document.querySelector('#status') looks for the element with id status. A selector should describe the intended target as precisely and simply as the page design allows. Code must account for the possibility of null before trying to use the returned value. querySelector() is useful for one target; it does not return every matching element. Other selection APIs exist, but they are not interchangeable merely because their names look similar. The important habit is to identify the node you intend to change, check that it was found, and then make the smallest appropriate update.

collegeVersion.heading: Reading and changing content
collegeVersion.body: Once code has an element reference, it can inspect or modify properties. The textContent property represents the text content of a node and its descendants. Assigning a string to element.textContent changes the element's text rather than asking the browser to interpret that string as HTML markup. That is a useful default when inserting ordinary labels, names, or counts. DOM code can also create an element with document.createElement('li'), set its textContent, and attach it with append(). Creating and attaching are separate steps: making a node alone does not put it into the visible document. These operations change the live DOM after the page has loaded; they do not rewrite the HTML file on disk. This lesson focuses on selecting and updating document nodes. User-event handlers, form processing, and data fetched from a server are separate topics that can later decide when or what to update.

collegeVersion.heading: A constrained update is easier to reason about
collegeVersion.body:
Consider an existing paragraph:

Waiting

. A script can obtain it with const status = document.querySelector('#status');. If status is not null, status.textContent = 'Ready'; changes only the paragraph's text. The selector identifies the target; the null check handles an absent target; textContent makes the intended kind of change clear. This is easier to audit than selecting a broad container and replacing all of its contents. It also separates data from markup: the string Ready is treated as text. DOM APIs can build rich interfaces, but reliable code still depends on a correct model of the tree, carefully scoped selection, and an appropriate mutation method. A developer can inspect the page before and after the statement and identify exactly which node changed. That narrow boundary makes a bug easier to diagnose and makes later maintenance less surprising. It also reduces accidental changes to headings, controls, and neighboring content whose structure is unrelated to the current task. Specific selection is therefore a design choice as well as a debugging habit for shared, long-lived pages and teams.

vocabulary.definition: A browser API that represents a document's structure in memory as objects and nodes that scripts can access.
An item in the DOM tree, such as a document, element, text item, or comment.
A DOM node representing an HTML element, with properties and possible child nodes.
A node that directly contains another node in the DOM tree.
A node directly contained by another node.
A pattern used to match elements; DOM selection APIs can use these patterns.
A Document method that returns the first element matching a specified CSS selector, or null when none matches.
A node property representing the text content of that node and its descendants.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine the browser turns a web page into a family tree it can keep on its desk. The page is not just a long sentence anymore: it has parts, and parts can contain smaller parts. JavaScript can ask for one part by name, read its text, or replace its text. For example, it can find the paragraph named status and change Waiting to Ready. It needs the exact label so it does not change a different part by accident.
eli10.analogy: The DOM is like a labeled tree of storage boxes. A box can hold smaller boxes or a note. A precise label helps you open just the box you mean to change. Putting new text on the note changes what someone reads in that box.
eli10.analogyLimits: A DOM tree is a programming representation, not a physical tree or a collection of independent boxes. Nodes have browser-defined behavior and properties, and changing the DOM may change what is displayed without changing the original HTML file.

workedExample:
Start with

Waiting

. The selector '#status' means “the element whose id is status.” In a browser script, const status = document.querySelector('#status'); either returns that paragraph element or null. The guard if (status) checks the latter case. Then status.textContent = 'Ready'; assigns text to the selected node. The resulting visible paragraph is Ready. This update does not create a new paragraph, does not react to an event, and does not interpret Ready as HTML; it modifies the text content of the already selected element.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling the DOM another name for HTML.
commonMistakes.correction: HTML is markup; the DOM is the browser's in-memory object model built from a document.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming querySelector() always returns an element.
commonMistakes.correction: It returns null when no element matches, so check before using the result.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting querySelector() to return every match.
commonMistakes.correction: It returns the first matching element; use an API designed for multiple results when that is the goal.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating textContent as a way to parse markup.
commonMistakes.correction: Use textContent for text; it does not ask the browser to interpret the assigned string as HTML.

compareContrast.distinction: HTML is markup text; the DOM is the browser's object representation of a document.
querySelector() finds an element; textContent reads or changes node text.

keyTakeaway: The DOM gives scripts a tree-shaped representation of a document. Select a specific node, handle the possibility that it is absent, and use a narrow update such as textContent when text is what you intend to change.

title: Events
in30Seconds: A browser event is an object that signals an occurrence, such as a user activating a button or a page finishing a load. Code can register an event listener with `addEventListener()` so a callback runs when a matching event is dispatched. The event object tells the listener about that occurrence. Some cancelable events also have a default browser action that a listener can prevent deliberately.
whyItMatters: Events connect JavaScript to what happens in a page. They let an interface respond to an activation, a keystroke, a loaded resource, or another platform occurrence without repeatedly checking every element. Understanding listener registration, the event object, and default actions helps students trace behavior responsibly. It also creates a base for later topics on forms, the DOM, accessibility, asynchronous work, and event delegation without treating those larger subjects as interchangeable.
learningObjectives: Define an event, event target, event listener, and callback.
Explain how `addEventListener()` associates a callback with an event type.
Distinguish `event.target` from `event.currentTarget` in a listener.
Predict the effect of `preventDefault()` on a cancelable default action.
Apply a listener to a small event-driven scenario.

collegeVersion.heading: Events and event targets
collegeVersion.body:
The DOM Standard describes events as objects dispatched to objects to signal an occurrence, including user interaction and network activity. An object that implements the `EventTarget` interface can have event listeners. In ordinary page code, elements such as a button are familiar event targets, but the idea is broader: `window`, `document`, and some other web-platform objects can also receive events. The event has a type, such as `click` or `load`. A listener is registered for a particular type, so a listener for `click` is not a general instruction to run on every possible occurrence.

The usual registration API is `target.addEventListener(type, callback, options)`. The `type` is a string naming the event type, and the callback is code the platform calls when a matching event reaches that listener. Registering the listener does not run the callback immediately. The callback runs later when the relevant event is dispatched. This separation is the core event-driven pattern: first describe what should happen, then let the platform invoke it when the occurrence happens. This lesson focuses on that basic pattern, rather than on selecting DOM elements, form validation, or security handling.

collegeVersion.heading: The event object and listener context
collegeVersion.body:
When the listener callback is invoked, it normally receives an event object. The object carries information about the particular event. Its `type` identifies the event type. Its `target` is the object to which the event was dispatched. Its `currentTarget` is the object whose listener is currently being invoked. These can be the same in a simple direct listener. They can differ when an event travels through a document tree and a listener is attached on an ancestor: the descendant that originated the event can be `target`, while the ancestor handling the listener can be `currentTarget`.

The DOM event model includes capture, target, and bubble phases. Many beginner listeners use the default option, which does not request capture. For common bubbling events, an event can then be observed by a listener on an ancestor after it is handled at its target. That fact supports a later pattern called event delegation, but delegation is not required to understand a single listener. More importantly, `target` should not be treated as a synonym for the element where every listener was registered. Read the event object and the registration site together. A listener can also be removed with `removeEventListener()` when supplied the matching type, callback, and relevant capture setting; this helps avoid behavior that should no longer be active.

collegeVersion.heading: Default actions and cancellation
collegeVersion.body:
Some events are cancelable and have a default action supplied by the user agent. For example, following a link after an activation is a familiar default action. Calling `event.preventDefault()` tells the user agent not to perform that default action for a cancelable event. It does not stop other listeners from running, and it does not automatically stop the event from moving through the event path. Those are separate concerns: `stopPropagation()` concerns propagation, while `preventDefault()` concerns a default action. A call to `preventDefault()` on a non-cancelable event has no effect on a default action.

Cancel a default action only when code provides an intentional alternative. For instance, a client-side interaction might manage an action itself, but an ordinary link should not be blocked simply because a listener exists. This is especially relevant for keyboard and assistive-technology use: behavior should preserve a meaningful, operable control rather than replacing it with an unannounced side effect. `addEventListener()` is generally preferable to assigning an `on...` property when code needs multiple independently registered listeners, because the API maintains an event-listener list. A listener callback should do focused work, use the event data it needs, and avoid assuming that every event shares the same cancelability, target, or propagation behavior.

vocabulary.definition: An object dispatched by the platform to signal an occurrence.
An object that can have event listeners and can be involved in event dispatch.
A registered callback that observes a specified event type on an event target.
A function supplied to an API so that the API can invoke it later.
The string that identifies a category of event, such as `click` or `load`.
Behavior the user agent performs for a cancelable event unless it is prevented.
Describes an event for which `preventDefault()` can signal that its default action should not occur.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: An event is like a small notice that says something happened. A button can send a notice when someone activates it. A listener is the instruction you leave with the button: when that kind of notice arrives, run this little job. The listener gets an event object, like the notice card itself, so it can inspect what happened. Some notices would normally trigger a built-in browser action. If the event is cancelable, code can say `preventDefault()` to stop that built-in action—but only when it has a clear replacement.
eli10.analogy: Imagine a school office has notice boards for different announcements. You pin a specific instruction under the ‘fire drill’ board, not under every board. When a drill notice arrives, the office follows that instruction. The notice says what kind of announcement it is and where it began. Some announcements have an automatic next step unless the office explicitly cancels it.
eli10.analogyLimits: Browser events are software objects, not paper notices, and dispatch can follow capture and bubble rules through a document tree. A browser default action also has precise platform rules; it is not an office worker freely choosing what to do.

workedExample: This listener has one job: record a cancelable `save` event and prevent its default action. `const target = new EventTarget(); const log = []; target.addEventListener("save", event => { log.push(event.type); event.preventDefault(); }); const allowed = target.dispatchEvent(new Event("save", { cancelable: true }));` When this exact code was run with Bun, `log` became `["save"]` and `allowed` was `false`. The callback ran because its registered type matched the dispatched event. The result was false because the event was cancelable and the listener called `preventDefault()`. In a page, the target might instead be a button and the event might be a browser-dispatched `click`; this example isolates the event mechanics without needing a page or a form.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting `addEventListener()` to execute the callback while registering it.
commonMistakes.correction: Registration records the callback; invocation occurs when a matching event is dispatched.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling `preventDefault()` to stop all other listeners.
commonMistakes.correction: It addresses a cancelable default action; it does not by itself stop propagation or other listeners.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming `event.target` always names the object whose listener is running.
commonMistakes.correction: Compare `target` with `currentTarget`, especially when an ancestor has the listener.

commonMistakes.mistake: Blocking a native action without offering an intentional replacement.
commonMistakes.correction: Prevent a default action only when the resulting interaction remains purposeful and operable.

compareContrast.distinction: `target` is the object to which the event was dispatched; `currentTarget` is the object whose listener is currently being invoked.
The first prevents a cancelable default action; the second addresses event propagation and does not itself cancel a default action.

keyTakeaway: Use `addEventListener()` to register focused callbacks for named event types. Inspect the event object, and prevent a cancelable default action only when the interaction has a deliberate alternative.

questionBank.prompt: What does `addEventListener("click", handler)` primarily do?
options: Runs `handler` immediately
Registers `handler` to observe matching click events
Changes every event into a click
Cancels the browser's click behavior
questionBank.explanation: It registers a listener for the named type; the callback is invoked later if a matching event is dispatched. Registration neither runs the callback immediately nor automatically cancels a default action.

questionBank.prompt: A listener is attached to a parent element, but a child element is the event's dispatch target. Which property identifies the parent while that parent's listener runs?
options: `event.currentTarget`
`event.target`
`event.defaultPrevented`
`event.type`
questionBank.explanation: During that listener invocation, `currentTarget` is the parent with the listener. `target` identifies the object to which the event was dispatched, here the child.

questionBank.prompt: What is the direct purpose of `event.preventDefault()` on a cancelable event?
options: Remove every listener
Rename the event type
Tell the user agent not to perform the event's default action
Force the event to bubble
questionBank.explanation: For a cancelable event, it prevents the default action. It does not remove listeners, rename an event, or itself control propagation.

questionBank.prompt: A script calls `preventDefault()` inside a listener for an event whose `cancelable` property is false. What should the programmer expect?

The listener is removed
All propagation stops
No default action is prevented by that call
questionBank.explanation: A non-cancelable event cannot have its default action prevented through `preventDefault()`. The call does not remove the listener or stop propagation.

questionBank.prompt: Which design is the clearest use of an event listener?
options: Register a callback that updates a status message when a matching event occurs
Put a long-running loop in the listener to check every possible event
Call `preventDefault()` for every event as a precaution
Treat every event target as the same element
questionBank.explanation: A focused callback for a matching occurrence is the event-driven pattern. The other choices either block behavior indiscriminately or make unsupported assumptions.

title: Form Validation and Submission
in30Seconds: HTML can describe constraints such as required fields, an email-shaped value, or a minimum length. Browsers can use those constraints to give immediate feedback before ordinary form submission. That feedback improves the interaction, but it is not a security boundary: the receiving server must validate every submitted value again before relying on it. Good validation also makes errors understandable, connected to the relevant field, and usable without depending only on color.
whyItMatters: Validation has two distinct jobs. On the client, it helps someone correct an entry while the form is in front of them. On the server, it protects the application’s rules and data when a request arrives. Keeping those jobs separate avoids a costly misunderstanding: browser checks are useful, but requests are not guaranteed to come through a particular page or browser. Clear accessible error feedback also reduces abandonment and makes a form usable with keyboards and assistive technology.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between browser-side constraint validation and server-side validation.
Apply required, type, minlength, and pattern only as appropriate input constraints.
Use checkValidity() and reportValidity() for their distinct browser behaviors.
Design an error message that identifies the field and correction needed.
Trace a form submission without treating client checks as a trust boundary.

collegeVersion.heading: Constraints describe an acceptable browser input
collegeVersion.body: HTML’s constraint-validation model lets authors state some ordinary requirements in markup. `required` says that a value must be supplied for controls to which it applies. `type="email"` asks the browser to apply its email-address validity rules; it does not prove that an address belongs to a particular person. `minlength` and `maxlength` place limits on text that a user edits, while `pattern` can add a regular-expression constraint when a well-defined format is genuinely needed. A constraint is not a substitute for a clear label, instructions, or an explanation of why a field is requested. It is also not a database schema. The browser evaluates a control’s validity as a client-side feature and can expose a `ValidityState` explaining categories such as missing value, type mismatch, or too-short value. The practical goal is to prevent predictable accidental errors early, not to write a miniature security policy in attributes. Use the smallest set of constraints that accurately reflects the user-facing requirement. Overly strict formats can reject legitimate names, addresses, or international data and turn validation into an obstacle rather than assistance.

collegeVersion.heading: Validation APIs and submission behavior
collegeVersion.body: A form normally performs interactive constraint validation when a user submits it. JavaScript can also ask whether constraints pass with `form.checkValidity()`. That method returns a Boolean and dispatches invalid events for invalid controls, but it does not display the browser’s validation message. `form.reportValidity()` also returns a Boolean and asks the user agent to report invalid controls to the user. These APIs are useful when a page has a deliberate interaction flow, but custom scripting should not suppress the browser’s useful semantics without replacing them with an equivalent accessible experience. The `submit` event is a good place to decide whether application-specific client feedback is needed; calling `preventDefault()` stops that submission event’s default action. Programmatic `form.submit()` differs from a user-initiated submission because it does not perform constraint validation and does not fire the submit event. The `requestSubmit()` method follows the submitter path instead. These details matter when testing: a green scripted path can accidentally skip the exact browser check the author expected.

collegeVersion.heading: Accessible error feedback is part of the interface
collegeVersion.body: An error state should tell a person what happened and how to repair it. WAI guidance recommends describing errors in text, identifying the affected field, and preserving enough context for someone to find it. Color alone is not sufficient because people perceive color differently and may not see a visual change. A useful pattern has a visible label, concise instructions before a field when needed, and an error message placed near the control after validation. When a form has multiple errors, an error summary near the beginning can identify the problem fields and link to them, while the field-level message supplies the specific repair. Error messages must remain accurate: ‘Enter an email address in the form name@example.com’ is actionable, whereas ‘Invalid input’ is vague. Authors should test keyboard focus and screen-reader announcements rather than assuming an ARIA attribute fixes a weak structure. Native labels and controls provide the foundation; ARIA can communicate dynamically added status only when it is used with an understood interaction design.

collegeVersion.heading: The server is the authority after submission
collegeVersion.body: Client-side validation is exposed to the person using the page, so it cannot be the final decision about whether data is allowed. A person can alter markup, turn off scripts, or send an HTTP request by another route. The server must therefore treat every received value as untrusted input: check required business rules, expected type and range, authorization, and any format the application truly requires before performing an action or storing data. This is not a reason to omit browser validation. The two layers solve different problems: client feedback reduces routine mistakes and unnecessary round trips, while server validation protects the application’s integrity. A server should return a clear error response when its validation fails, because even a careful browser form can be stale or incomplete. Do not put secrets in client-side constraints or assume a hidden or disabled control establishes authorization. Form controls influence a browser’s interface and submission entry list; they do not decide what a server permits. Designing the boundary explicitly makes both the user experience and the defensive model easier to reason about.

vocabulary.definition: The browser feature that evaluates applicable HTML form-control constraints before or during interactive validation.
A form-control attribute that makes an otherwise empty value invalid when the control is a candidate for validation.
The browser-exposed collection of flags describing whether a control fails a particular validity condition.
A method that evaluates constraints and returns whether they pass without asking the browser to show validation messages.
A method that evaluates constraints and asks the browser to report invalid controls to the user.
Feedback or checks performed in the browser before a request reaches the receiving application.
Verification by the receiving application that submitted data meets its rules before the application relies on it.
A message near the start of a form that identifies one or more submission problems and can guide a person to them.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: A form can have rules like ‘this box cannot be empty’ or ‘this needs to look like an email address.’ The browser can point out a broken rule before it sends the form. That is helpful coaching, but it is not a locked door. The place that receives the form must check the answers too, because someone can send a request without using the page. Error messages should say which answer needs changing and what to do.
eli10.analogy: Think of a school worksheet and a teacher. The worksheet can circle a blank answer before it is handed in. The teacher still reads the sheet and checks the answers, because a student could hand in a different sheet or make a mistake the circle did not catch.
eli10.analogyLimits: Browsers do not judge whether information is true in the way a teacher judges answers. They apply defined technical constraints. A server’s checks are also application rules, not a guarantee that every real-world statement is true.

workedExample: A newsletter form contains `<input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>` and a visible `<label for="email">Email address</label>`. If the person submits it empty, interactive browser validation can identify the missing required value. If they enter `hello`, the email type can produce a type-mismatch result. A script could call `form.checkValidity()` to decide whether constraints pass, or `form.reportValidity()` to request browser feedback. Neither call means the server may trust the request. When the server receives an email value, it must still apply the application’s own validation before creating a subscription. If the server rejects it, the page should present a specific text error associated with the email field, not only a red outline.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a required attribute as a server security control.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the attribute for browser feedback, but validate the required rule again on the server.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using pattern for every text field.
commonMistakes.correction: Use a pattern only for a stable, well-understood user-facing format; unnecessary patterns reject valid input.

commonMistakes.mistake: Showing errors only by changing a border color.
commonMistakes.correction: Provide clear text that identifies the field and the needed correction.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling submit() while expecting normal constraint validation.
commonMistakes.correction: Understand that submit() bypasses interactive validation; use the appropriate flow and test it.

compareContrast.distinction: Both evaluate constraints; reportValidity() additionally asks the browser to report invalid controls.
Client checks improve immediate feedback; server checks are required before the application relies on received data.
required rejects an empty required value, while minlength constrains a nonempty user-entered value's length.

keyTakeaway: HTML constraints and browser feedback help people correct routine mistakes, but they are not authorization or data-integrity controls. Use accessible, specific error messages and require the receiving server to validate every submitted value.

questionBank.prompt: What is the server’s role when a browser form uses required fields?
options: It may trust the browser’s checks as final
It only needs to validate values from mobile browsers
It must validate received values before relying on them
It should remove client-side feedback
questionBank.explanation: A request can arrive without following client-side checks, so the receiving application must validate it. Client feedback remains useful but is not the final authority.

questionBank.prompt: Which method asks the browser to show feedback for invalid controls?
options: checkValidity()
requestSubmit()
submit()
reportValidity()
questionBank.explanation: reportValidity() evaluates constraints and requests browser reporting. checkValidity() evaluates without that reporting; the submission methods have different behavior.

questionBank.prompt: A form marks an account name invalid only with a red border. What improvement best addresses the main accessibility problem?
options: Add a text message explaining the field and correction
Make the red border thicker
Remove the label to reduce clutter
Replace the input with a generic div
questionBank.explanation: Text that identifies the problem and correction does not depend only on color. A border alone is not sufficient feedback, and the other choices weaken semantics.

questionBank.prompt: What does minlength="8" do when an optional text control is left empty?
options: It makes the empty field valid only after eight characters are entered
It encrypts the value before submission
It makes the empty field invalid because minlength implies required
It prevents the server from receiving the field
questionBank.explanation: minlength does not imply required. An optional empty control can be valid; if a user enters a value, the applicable minimum length matters.

questionBank.prompt: Why is calling form.submit() a risky shortcut when testing required fields?
options: It changes every input into a hidden field
It bypasses constraint validation and does not fire the submit event
It sends the form only with GET
It automatically validates the server response
questionBank.explanation: The HTML standard distinguishes submit() from a submission path that performs validation. It does not alter fields, force GET, or validate a response.

title: Fetch API Basics
in30Seconds: The browser Fetch API lets JavaScript request a resource over the network. Calling fetch(url) returns a Promise, so the response arrives later rather than as an immediate value. When that Promise resolves, inspect the Response before reading its body: response.ok tells you whether its status is in the 200–299 range. Then a method such as response.json() can read and parse JSON data. A 404 response is still a response, so it needs an explicit check.
whyItMatters: Fetch connects a page to data and services beyond its original HTML: course projects may load a public data file, and production interfaces may request an application’s own endpoint. The important reasoning skill is separating transport from success. A request can reach a server and still receive a 404 or 500 response. Checking the response deliberately gives a user-facing program a clear place to choose a message or fallback. This lesson keeps the boundary narrow: requesting public data, examining a response, parsing JSON, and reporting ordinary failures without handling credentials or private information.
learningObjectives: Define fetch() as a Promise-based browser request API.
Distinguish a network/request rejection from an HTTP error response.
Use Response.ok to evaluate a basic successful HTTP response.
Explain why response.json() is asynchronous.
Apply a check-before-parse pattern to a public JSON request.

collegeVersion.heading: A request begins an asynchronous operation
collegeVersion.body: The Fetch API is a browser interface for requesting resources. The global fetch() function accepts a resource location and optional request settings, then returns a Promise. A Promise represents a result that is not available at the moment the call is made. This matters because a browser must allow time for a request to travel, a server to respond, and response headers to arrive. Code therefore does not write const data = fetch(url) and expect data immediately. Instead, it uses await inside an async function or attaches Promise handlers. When fetch resolves, its value is a Response object. That object describes the HTTP response and provides methods for reading its body. Fetch is an API supplied by the browser environment; JavaScript supplies the async and await language features used to organize the waiting. This lesson uses a public relative path such as /data/message.json as a safe example. A real application must choose resources it is authorized to request and should not put secrets into client-side code.

collegeVersion.heading: A response is not automatically a successful result
collegeVersion.body: A frequent mistake is to treat a resolved fetch Promise as proof that an application got useful data. MDN documents an important boundary: fetch rejects for failures such as a malformed URL or a network failure, but it does not reject merely because the server answers with an HTTP error status such as 404 or 500. In both the successful and error-status cases, the browser has received an HTTP response, so fetch can resolve to a Response. The Response has a status number and an ok Boolean. The ok property is true when the status is from 200 through 299; otherwise it is false. A simple program can check if (!response.ok) and throw its own Error before parsing. That converts an unacceptable HTTP result into the program’s chosen error path. It does not diagnose every cause of failure, and it does not make a retry, authentication, or security policy. It simply preserves the distinction between ‘a response arrived’ and ‘this code accepts that response as successful.’

collegeVersion.heading: Reading JSON is a second asynchronous step
collegeVersion.body: A Response body is not already a JavaScript object. If an endpoint sends JSON, response.json() reads the body and parses it as JSON, returning another Promise. That is why the common await sequence has two awaits: first await fetch(url), then await response.json(). Checking ok before the second step avoids presenting an error page as though it were expected data. For a small public response shaped as {"message": "Hello"}, the parsed value can be assigned to data and data.message can be displayed as text. The data shape still matters: a syntactically valid JSON value might be an array, a number, or an object without a message field. Robust applications validate the shape needed by their interface. Parsing also can fail if the body is not valid JSON, so a surrounding try/catch is appropriate for a small user-facing example. Keep user text separate from HTML markup when rendering it; a DOM topic covers safe text updates. Fetch/API basics ends at a clear boundary: request, assess response, parse expected public data, and communicate failure.

collegeVersion.heading: A small pattern with visible decisions
collegeVersion.body: Consider an async loadMessage function. It requests /data/message.json, checks response.ok, parses JSON, and assigns data.message to an already selected element’s textContent. Each line has a different role. The fetch call starts the request. The ok condition applies the application’s acceptance rule. json() consumes and parses the body. The final textContent assignment presents a known field as text. The catch block covers a rejected request, a thrown HTTP-status error, or a JSON parsing error and supplies a general message. This pattern is intentionally modest. It does not send a password, add an authorization header, assume every endpoint returns JSON, or claim that fetch alone solves cross-origin access. Those are separate design and security concerns. The value of the pattern is that a reader can trace each outcome: acceptable response and expected data display a message; an unacceptable response or parsing/request problem produces a controlled status message.

vocabulary.definition: Browser interfaces for making network requests and working with their responses.
A function that starts a fetch request and returns a Promise for a Response.
An object representing the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation.
An object representing the HTTP response to a fetch request, including status and body-reading methods.
A numeric code in an HTTP response that communicates the result category.
A Response Boolean that is true when its status is from 200 through 299.
A text data format commonly used to represent structured values.
A Response method that reads its body and returns a Promise for JSON-parsed data.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine asking a library desk to bring you a book. You get a claim ticket first, not the book right away. Fetch gives JavaScript a claim ticket called a Promise. Later, the desk may hand back a book, or it may hand back a note saying the book was not found. Both are replies from the desk. That is why code must look at the reply before treating it as the book it wanted. If the reply is okay, json() is like opening the book and reading its organized information.
eli10.analogy: Fetch is like ordering a labeled package: the Promise is the tracking slip, the Response is the package that arrives, response.ok is the inspection label, and json() is opening a package expected to contain structured information.
eli10.analogyLimits: Network requests do not follow a single delivery route, and an HTTP response is not a physical package. A status code describes a protocol result, while parsing JSON is a software operation that can fail independently.

workedExample:
Assume a page already has

Loading…

and a public file at /data/message.json containing {"message":"Welcome"}. An async function gets the status element, then runs const response = await fetch('/data/message.json');. If !response.ok, it throws new Error('Request failed');. Otherwise it runs const data = await response.json(); and sets status.textContent = data.message. If the file is missing and the server returns 404, fetch can still resolve, but response.ok is false, so the code follows the catch path and can show ‘Could not load message.’ The same catch also handles a rejected request or invalid JSON. This example deliberately handles no credentials, headers, or private data.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming fetch rejects for every 404 or 500 response.
commonMistakes.correction: Inspect response.ok or response.status because an HTTP error response can still resolve fetch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a Response as if it were parsed data.
commonMistakes.correction: Read the body with an appropriate asynchronous method such as response.json().

commonMistakes.mistake: Parsing before deciding whether the HTTP response is acceptable.
commonMistakes.correction: Apply the application’s response check before reading expected data.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating arbitrary JSON as the exact object the interface expects.
commonMistakes.correction: Check the fields and shape required by the program before using them.

compareContrast.distinction: A rejection reflects request/network failure; an HTTP error response can resolve to Response and needs an explicit status check.
ok evaluates a response’s status range; json() consumes and parses its body.

keyTakeaway: fetch() starts an asynchronous request and yields a Response, not immediately usable JSON. Check response.ok, then parse the body you expect, and handle request, status, and parsing failures as separate possibilities.

questionBank.prompt: What does fetch('/data/message.json') return immediately?
options: A Promise
A parsed JavaScript object
A completed Response body
An HTTP status number
questionBank.explanation: fetch() returns a Promise. A Response and any parsed data are available later through asynchronous handling.

questionBank.prompt: Why should code check response.ok after awaiting fetch()?
options: It turns JSON into HTML
It detects whether the status is in the 200–299 range
It guarantees the network is offline
It creates a new request
questionBank.explanation: response.ok is true for 200–299 statuses. It neither parses JSON nor creates a request.

questionBank.prompt: A server returns HTTP 404. Which outcome is possible for fetch()?
options: It must reject before producing a Response
It must parse JSON automatically
It can resolve to a Response whose ok is false
It changes the status to 200
questionBank.explanation: HTTP error statuses can still produce a resolved Response; ok is false outside the 200–299 range.

questionBank.prompt: After an acceptable JSON response, which statement obtains parsed data?
options: const data = response.ok;
const data = fetch(response);
const data = response.status;
const data = await response.json();
questionBank.explanation: response.json() reads and parses the body asynchronously. ok and status are metadata, while fetch starts a request.

questionBank.prompt: Which order best handles a public JSON request?
options: Parse JSON, then start fetch, then check status
Await fetch, check response.ok, then await response.json()
Check response.ok before fetch, then parse HTML
Await response.json() without obtaining a Response
questionBank.explanation: First obtain the Response, assess whether the application accepts its status, and then parse the expected body. The other sequences use values before they exist or choose the wrong operation.

title: Async Programming
in30Seconds: Asynchronous JavaScript starts an operation and lets the surrounding program continue instead of waiting for every result immediately. A Promise represents the operation's eventual outcome. You can use `.then()` and `.catch()` to handle fulfillment and rejection, or write an `async` function and use `await` inside it. `await` pauses that async function at one point; it does not turn the whole program into a stop sign.
whyItMatters: Web programs often need to coordinate work whose result is not available right away. Promises give that later result—and a possible failure—a defined path through the program. Learning the model helps a student read JavaScript without assuming that the next line always receives a finished value. It also builds habits that matter beyond a browser: return promises deliberately, handle failures near the operation that can explain them, and avoid making independent work wait needlessly.
learningObjectives: Define Promise, pending, fulfilled, rejected, and settled.
Trace a simple promise chain including a rejection handler.
Explain what `async` changes about a function's return value.
Apply `await` with `try...catch` to handle a rejected operation.
Distinguish sequential work from independent work that may be started together.

collegeVersion.heading: Promises describe a result that is not ready yet
collegeVersion.body:
A Promise is a JavaScript object representing the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation and its resulting value. It has an initial pending state. A pending promise has not yet produced a final outcome. It later becomes fulfilled, carrying a fulfillment value, or rejected, carrying a reason such as an Error. Once it is fulfilled or rejected, it is settled: its state will not change again. A promise is therefore not the completed value itself. If a function returns a promise, code that calls the function receives an object that describes a future outcome, not a shortcut around waiting for that outcome.

Handlers say what to do after that outcome. `promise.then(onFulfilled)` registers work for fulfillment, while `promise.catch(onRejected)` registers work for rejection. A useful chain returns values or promises from each handler, so the next link receives the appropriate eventual value. `then()` itself returns a new promise. That detail is why a chain can express consecutive steps without nesting one handler inside another. A rejection can come from the original operation, from an explicit `throw`, or from an error thrown by a handler. Ending a chain with `catch()` gives one place to handle an unhandled rejection from an earlier link. This lesson uses locally created promises so the model stays separate from the later Fetch/API topic.

collegeVersion.heading: async functions and await use the same promise model
collegeVersion.body:
Putting `async` before a function declaration or expression makes an async function. Calling an async function always returns a Promise, even when the body appears to `return` an ordinary value. If the body returns `42`, the returned promise fulfills with `42`; if an error escapes the body, the returned promise rejects with that error. The caller can still use `.then()` and `.catch()` on the result. This is a common beginner trap: `const result = makeLabel()` is a promise if `makeLabel` is async, not the label that its body will later produce.

Inside an async function, `await expression` evaluates the expression and waits for its promise-like result to settle before continuing that async function. On fulfillment, the await expression produces the fulfillment value. On rejection, it throws the rejection reason at that line. `try...catch` therefore works naturally around awaited work: put the steps that might reject in `try`, and decide in `catch` how to report, recover, or rethrow the error. Handling an error does not mean silently hiding it. A good handler gives useful context or deliberately passes the error onward when the current function cannot make a sound recovery decision. In normal non-module code, `await` belongs inside an async function; modules also permit top-level await, but module loading is outside this lesson.

collegeVersion.heading: Choose ordering from dependencies, not from habit
collegeVersion.body:
`await` makes sequential code readable, but it also means the next awaited expression does not begin until execution reaches it. That is correct when a later step needs the earlier result: compute a student ID first, then use that ID to make a label. It is unnecessarily slow when two tasks are independent. For independent promises, start both operations first and then coordinate their results. `Promise.all([first, second])` returns one promise that fulfills with an array of values in the same order as its input when every input fulfills. If an input rejects, the returned promise rejects.

This is not an instruction to run every operation concurrently. Dependencies, resource limits, and error policy determine the appropriate design. The important reasoning step is to ask whether the next operation needs the prior operation's value. If yes, await in sequence. If no, starting work before awaiting can avoid accidental serial delay. In either style, keep the promise boundary visible. Do not write a function that begins asynchronous work and then claim it already has the final value. Return the promise, await it in an async caller, or attach explicit handlers. Those choices make success and failure paths inspectable in tests and easier for a teammate to understand.

vocabulary.definition: An object representing the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation and its resulting value.
The initial promise state before it has fulfilled or rejected.
The state of a promise that completed successfully with a value.
The state of a promise that completed unsuccessfully with a reason.
No longer pending: a promise has either fulfilled or rejected.
A function whose call returns a Promise and whose body can use await.
An operator that pauses an async function at an expression until its promise-like operand settles.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine asking a library helper to find a book in storage. You get a claim ticket now, not the book. The ticket is like a Promise: it will later lead to either the book being ready or a notice that something went wrong. You can leave instructions for each outcome. An `async` function is a helper who works with those tickets. When it uses `await`, that one helper pauses at a ticket until it is resolved, then continues with the book or handles the problem. Other people in the library can still keep working.
eli10.analogy: A Promise is a library claim ticket. `.then()` is an instruction for what to do when the book arrives; `.catch()` is an instruction for a problem. `await` is the helper waiting at that one counter for the ticket's result.
eli10.analogyLimits: A JavaScript promise is not a physical ticket and does not guarantee a particular time. Also, `await` pauses an async function's progress, not a person or every task in the program.

workedExample: This Bun-verified program has no network work: `async function labelJob() { const label = await Promise.resolve("ready"); return label.toUpperCase(); } labelJob().then(console.log); Promise.reject(new Error("paused")).catch(error => console.log(error.message)); console.log("started");`. Bun printed `started`, then `paused`, then `READY`. `labelJob()` immediately returned a promise, so the program could print `started` before its awaited fulfillment continuation ran. The separate rejected promise called its `catch` handler. Inside `labelJob`, `await` turned the fulfilled value `"ready"` into `label`; the async function's `return` fulfilled its own promise with `"READY"`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a Promise as if it were already its fulfilled value.
commonMistakes.correction: Await it in an async function or attach a fulfillment handler before using its eventual value.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using `await` outside an async function in a normal script.
commonMistakes.correction: Place it inside an async function; top-level await is a separate module feature.

commonMistakes.mistake: Handling only success in a chain that can reject.
commonMistakes.correction: Add a considered `catch()` or use `try...catch` around awaited work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Awaiting independent operations one after another by default.
commonMistakes.correction: When their results do not depend on each other, start them first and coordinate with an appropriate promise combinator such as `Promise.all`.

compareContrast.distinction: A fulfilled promise has a successful value; a rejected promise has a failure reason.
Both handle promise outcomes; the latter lets an async function express the failure path with statement syntax.
Sequential awaits fit dependent steps; Promise.all coordinates promises that can be started independently.

keyTakeaway: Promises make later success and failure explicit. Async functions still return promises; `await` unwraps a settled result only inside the async function, where `try...catch` can handle rejection.

questionBank.prompt: Which state describes a Promise before it has fulfilled or rejected?
options: pending
returned
awaited
settled
questionBank.explanation: Pending is the initial state. A settled promise has already fulfilled or rejected; returned and awaited are not Promise states.

questionBank.prompt: What does calling an async function return immediately?
options: Its eventual ordinary value
A Promise
Only an Error
Nothing until every task ends
questionBank.explanation: An async function call returns a Promise. That promise may later fulfill with a returned value or reject with an uncaught error.

questionBank.prompt: Inside an async function, a Promise used with await rejects. What happens at the await expression?
options: It silently becomes undefined
It automatically retries
Its rejection reason is thrown
The whole JavaScript program stops
questionBank.explanation: A rejected awaited promise throws its rejection reason at the await expression, so surrounding try...catch can handle it. It does not automatically retry or stop the whole program.

questionBank.prompt: A promise chain has several consecutive then handlers. Which addition can handle a rejection from an earlier unhandled link?
options: A second pending state
A variable declaration
A return outside the chain
A catch handler at the end of the chain
questionBank.explanation: A catch handler at the end can receive an unhandled rejection from an earlier chain step. The other choices do not register rejection handling.

questionBank.prompt: Two operations are independent: neither needs the other's result. Which design avoids making the second wait merely because of code order?
options: Start both promises, then coordinate them with Promise.all
Await the first before starting the second
Convert both operations to ordinary values
Use catch before either operation starts
questionBank.explanation: Starting independent work first and then using Promise.all can coordinate both results without accidental serial waiting. Sequential await is appropriate when a later step depends on an earlier value.

title: The Web Platform
in30Seconds: The web platform is the shared set of web standards and browser-provided capabilities used to build sites and web applications. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are familiar parts of that environment, but browsers also expose Web APIs such as the DOM. Specifications describe expected behavior; browser teams implement that behavior. A web developer therefore needs to distinguish the JavaScript language from the browser capabilities that JavaScript can call.
whyItMatters: Calling everything “JavaScript” hides an important boundary. A language feature and a browser API have different specifications, availability, and fallback choices. In a course, that distinction makes it easier to read documentation and reason about why code works in a browser but not necessarily in another JavaScript environment. In practice, it helps teams select a capability deliberately, test for it when appropriate, and provide a useful baseline when it is unavailable.
learningObjectives: Define the web platform as standards plus browser-provided capabilities.
Distinguish JavaScript language features from Web APIs.
Explain the roles of a specification and a browser implementation.
Identify the DOM as a browser-provided interface created from a document.
Apply feature detection to choose a fallback path.

collegeVersion.heading: A platform, not one library
collegeVersion.body: The web platform is the environment in which a browser turns web resources into an interactive experience. It is not a package that a developer imports, and it is not another name for JavaScript. It includes interoperating technologies and the interfaces browsers make available to pages. HTML describes document markup; CSS describes presentation rules; JavaScript is a programming language used in many places, including browsers. In a browser, JavaScript can also call Web APIs. MDN describes Web APIs as interfaces available while developing a web app or site. The Document Object Model (DOM), for example, lets a script inspect and change the document that the browser has built. A page may use no JavaScript at all and still use the web platform through HTML and CSS. Conversely, JavaScript can run outside a browser, where a browser-specific object such as document may not exist. That difference is a useful diagnostic clue: ask whether a name belongs to the language itself or to the host environment. The platform is broad, but that does not mean every lesson must list every API. A sound mental model focuses on the boundary between specifications, browser implementations, and the particular capabilities a page chooses to use.

collegeVersion.heading: Standards describe behavior; browsers provide an implementation
collegeVersion.body: Web standards are technical agreements written as specifications. They describe concepts, data, algorithms, and required behavior so independent implementations can aim for compatible results. WHATWG's HTML Standard, for instance, specifies HTML and describes HTML user agents such as web browsers parsing markup into a DOM. A specification is not itself the browser running on a person's device. Browser engines and surrounding browser software implement specifications, ship versions over time, and may expose a capability differently depending on version, settings, permissions, or context. This is why careful documentation distinguishes a standard from observed support. A developer should avoid saying that a feature works “everywhere” merely because it worked in one browser. Instead, check the relevant documentation and define what the application should do when the desired capability is unavailable. Standards make interoperability possible; testing and fallbacks make a real application more resilient. The goal is not to memorize standards organizations. It is to recognize that a browser API has a defined contract and an implementation boundary, so requirements should be checked rather than guessed.

collegeVersion.heading: Interfaces are the bridge from code to browser capability
collegeVersion.body: An API is an application programming interface: a defined way for code to request a service or work with an object. Web APIs are commonly exposed as objects, methods, events, and interfaces. Web IDL is a standard language for describing such interfaces, which helps specifications state the names, inputs, outputs, and relationships that an implementation must provide. The DOM illustrates the arrangement. When a browser parses an HTML document, it creates a document representation; the DOM APIs expose that representation to scripts. A script can use document.querySelector in a browser because the browser provides document and the associated DOM interface. The method call uses JavaScript syntax, but the capability being invoked is supplied by the browser. Keeping those roles separate reduces confusion when reading error messages, documentation, or code examples. This lesson does not attempt to teach each API. Fetching data, handling events, storage, media, and accessibility each involve their own APIs and constraints. Here, the transferable skill is to locate the owning platform feature, read its contract, and decide whether it belongs in the application's supported baseline.

collegeVersion.heading: Use capabilities deliberately and detect them when a fallback exists
collegeVersion.body: A capability check asks whether the current environment provides the particular feature code plans to use. It is more reliable than guessing from a browser name or version because it tests the capability directly. A small example is checking whether geolocation is present before offering a location-based option: if ('geolocation' in navigator) { /* offer the optional feature */ } else { /* keep a manual location choice */ }. The check does not grant permission, guarantee a useful location, or replace error handling; it only establishes whether that API is exposed. The fallback should preserve the core task rather than leaving the person stranded. For a manual location choice, that might mean allowing a person to enter a city or postal code. This approach is often called progressive enhancement: begin with a useful base experience, then add an optional enhancement where the platform supports it. It also makes requirements visible to reviewers. A team can document which path is essential, which is optional, and how each is tested. Feature detection is not a reason to scatter checks everywhere or to avoid reading compatibility information. It is one tool for expressing an intentional boundary between the application and the capabilities supplied by the user's browser.

vocabulary.definition: The collection of web standards and browser capabilities used to create and run web pages and applications.
A browser-exposed interface that code in a web application can use to interact with a platform capability.
A technical document that defines expected behavior and interfaces for an implementation.
A concrete browser or other program that provides behavior described by a specification.
Software, such as a web browser, that obtains and processes web content.
A browser-provided object representation of a document that scripts can access.
An interface definition language used by web specifications to describe programming interfaces.
Testing whether a capability is available in the current environment before using it.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Think of a browser as a workshop that follows shared instruction books. HTML tells it about the page's pieces, CSS tells it how those pieces can look, and JavaScript lets code ask the workshop to do things. The workshop also provides special tools, called Web APIs. The DOM tool lets code look at the page the browser has built. Those special tools are not automatically part of JavaScript; they are tools the browser makes available. Different browser versions can have different tools or settings, so a careful page checks for an optional tool and still offers a useful basic path.
eli10.analogy: The web platform is like a set of common building codes plus the equipment in a workshop. The code says how a door should fit; each workshop builds actual doors and supplies its own tools. A builder can use a tool only if that workshop has it.
eli10.analogyLimits: Browsers are software implementations rather than workshops, and web standards can specify detailed algorithms, not merely general suggestions. The analogy also does not mean every browser exposes exactly the same optional capability at every time or permission setting.

workedExample: A transit page has an optional “Use my location” button and a manual station search. The developer treats the manual search as the core path. Before enabling the optional button, the page checks whether the browser exposes navigator.geolocation. If it does, the button can request location through that Web API; if it does not, the button is hidden or explained while the station search remains usable. The check does not assume that the user will grant permission or that a location request will succeed, so the page still handles those outcomes. JavaScript supplies the if statement and property check; the browser supplies navigator and its geolocation capability. This separation tells the team where to find the correct documentation and why a fallback belongs in the design.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling every browser capability “JavaScript.”
commonMistakes.correction: Separate JavaScript language syntax from Web APIs exposed by the browser.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a specification as proof that a feature is available in every current context.
commonMistakes.correction: Use the specification to understand behavior and check support or capabilities for the environments you support.

commonMistakes.mistake: Checking a browser name instead of the capability needed.
commonMistakes.correction: When an optional feature has a fallback, test for that feature directly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Making an optional API the only way to finish a core task.
commonMistakes.correction: Provide a baseline path, then enhance it when the browser offers the capability.

compareContrast.distinction: JavaScript is a programming language; a Web API is a browser-provided interface that JavaScript can call.
A specification defines expected behavior; an implementation is software that provides that behavior.
Feature detection checks the capability itself, while browser sniffing guesses from product identity or version.

keyTakeaway: The web platform combines standards with the capabilities browsers implement. Identify whether code relies on the JavaScript language or a Web API, then design a supported baseline and a deliberate optional path.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best describes a Web API?
options: A browser-exposed interface that a web application can use
A synonym for the JavaScript language specification
A CSS rule for arranging elements
A server-only database protocol
questionBank.explanation: Web APIs are interfaces exposed for web applications. JavaScript, CSS, and server protocols are distinct concepts.

questionBank.prompt: A browser parses an HTML page and exposes document.querySelector(). Which pairing is accurate?
options: HTML parsing is a JavaScript-only feature; querySelector is CSS
The browser provides the DOM API; JavaScript code can call it
The DOM is a replacement for HTML markup
A specification executes the method on the user's device
questionBank.explanation: Browsers parse HTML into a DOM and expose DOM APIs; JavaScript is commonly used to call them. The other choices confuse the roles.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing language, document model, and browser roles

questionBank.prompt: Why is feature detection usually preferable to deciding behavior from a browser name?
options: It guarantees that a person will grant permission
It makes all browsers implement every API
It tests whether the needed capability is available in the current environment
It converts an optional capability into a standard requirement
questionBank.explanation: Feature detection checks the actual capability. It cannot guarantee permission, create support, or turn an option into a requirement.

questionBank.prompt: What is the clearest difference between a web specification and a browser implementation?
options: A specification is a programming language, while an implementation is a stylesheet
A specification is a list of websites, while an implementation is a domain name
A specification applies only to servers, while an implementation applies only to phones
A specification defines expected behavior, while an implementation provides that behavior in software
questionBank.explanation: Specifications define expected behavior and interfaces; browsers implement them in software. The other pairings are inaccurate.

questionBank.prompt: A form's core task can be completed by typing a city, but a location API can prefill it when present. Which design is strongest?
options: Remove manual entry so every visitor uses the API
Use the manual entry as a baseline and add the API as an optional enhancement
Assume every browser exposes the API because it is standardized
Check only a browser brand and show no fallback
questionBank.explanation: A useful baseline plus an optional enhancement preserves the core task when the API is unavailable or unsuitable. The other designs rely on unsupported assumptions.

title: Accessibility
in30Seconds: Accessibility is a foundational concept in Web Development. This lesson introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it.
whyItMatters: College courses use accessibility as a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions.
learningObjectives: Define accessibility using course-appropriate language.
Identify important features and limits of accessibility.
Apply accessibility to a simple scenario.

collegeVersion.heading: The core idea
collegeVersion.body: Accessibility is a concept students use to organize information, ask better questions, and explain relationships in Web Development. A college-level explanation names the concept, describes its parts, and shows how those parts work together. Connect the term to the problem it helps people solve rather than treating it as a fact to memorize.

collegeVersion.heading: How to reason with it
collegeVersion.body: Start by identifying the setting, the relevant evidence, and the decision or explanation at stake. Then separate the central idea from examples, exceptions, and related vocabulary. This keeps the concept useful without making it broader or more certain than the available evidence supports.

vocabulary.definition: A foundational Web Development concept covered in this lesson.
The situation or conditions that shape how an idea is understood.
Information used to support or evaluate an explanation.
Using an idea to interpret a specific problem.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Think of accessibility as a label on a toolbox drawer. The label does not do the job by itself—it helps you choose the right tool for the problem.
eli10.analogy: Like reading a map legend before choosing a route, accessibility helps you understand what you are looking at first.

workedExample: A student reads a short Web Development scenario, identifies the details that matter, and explains how accessibility helps organize them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating accessibility as a definition to recite.
commonMistakes.correction: Use the definition together with context and an example.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming related terms mean exactly the same thing.
commonMistakes.correction: Compare their purpose and limits.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using one example as proof in every situation.
commonMistakes.correction: Check whether the example matches the question.

keyTakeaway: Accessibility is most useful when you can define it, recognize where it applies, and explain its limits.

quickCheck.prompt: Which approach best shows understanding of Accessibility?
options: Memorizing the term without context.
Defining it and applying it to an example.
Assuming it means every related term.
quickCheck.explanation: Understanding includes meaning and application.

quickCheck.prompt: Why is context important when using Accessibility?
options: It is never important.
It helps determine whether the concept fits the situation.
It replaces the definition.
quickCheck.explanation: Context helps determine whether an explanation is appropriate.

quickCheck.prompt: What should a careful college-level explanation include?
options: Only an opinion.
A term, evidence, and an application.
A long definition with no example.
quickCheck.explanation: Clear explanations link terminology, evidence, and application.
